This translational chemogenetic approach would represent the first human-applicable bidirectional receptor system for sleep-wake regulation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a thermoregulatory neuromodulation strategy that exploits the tight coupling between body temperature decline and sleep onset by targeting TRPM2-expressing warm-sensitive neurons in the preoptic area through precisely controlled, non-invasive peripheral thermal manipulation combined with pharmacological TRPM2 potentiation. A wearable device would deliver programmable warm or cool thermal stimuli to the distal skin (palms, feet) to exploit the glabrous skin arteriovenous anastomosis system: warming distal skin promotes vasodilation and core body temperature decline, facilitating sleep, while cooling reverses this process to promote arousal. Simultaneously, a topical or oral TRPM2-selective positive allosteric modulator would be administered to lower the activation threshold of preoptic warm-sensitive neurons, amplifying the sleep-permissive hypothermic signal at physiological temperatures. This dual peripheral-central approach avoids direct brain stimulation, leverages an endogenous thermoregulatory pathway resistant to tolerance, and achieves bidirectionality through simple thermal polarity switching. Feasibility is supported by evidence that TRPM2-POA neuron activation bidirectionally controls body temperature and sleep.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multi-scale computational digital-twin framework for optimizing personalized, tolerance-free sleep-wake neuromodulation. The system would integrate individual neuroanatomical MRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and resting-state EEG to construct subject-specific biophysical models of cortical and subcortical sleep-wake circuits, including thalamocortical loops, hypothalamic flip-flop switch dynamics, and brainstem ascending arousal pathways. Using neural mass models calibrated to each individual's baseline sleep architecture, the digital twin would simulate responses to candidate interventions—transcranial electrical stimulation, acoustic stimulation, focused ultrasound, or pharmacological agents—before any physical intervention is applied. A Bayesian optimization engine would iteratively refine stimulation parameters across nightly sessions, using prediction error between simulated and observed EEG as a learning signal to prevent habituation and maintain efficacy. This framework addresses the critical problem that existing one-size-fits-all neuromodulation protocols yield highly variable results, and would provide the first platform for in-silico pre-screening and continuous adaptation of multimodal sleep-wake interventions.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose constructing a pan-cancer "Glycan Tropism Atlas" by systematically profiling the N-glycome of circulating extracellular vesicles (EVs) from patients with known organ-specific metastases across multiple cancer types using lectin microarray and mass spectrometry glycomics. The central hypothesis is that tumor-derived EVs carry organ-destination-specific glycan signatures that mediate their uptake by resident cells in target organs, analogous to but distinct from the known integrin-based mechanisms. By training a multi-class machine learning classifier on EV glycan profiles from a discovery cohort stratified by metastatic site (lung, liver, bone, brain, peritoneum) and primary tumor type, we will derive a liquid biopsy-compatible glycan barcode predictive of organotropism. Classifier performance will be validated in an independent prospective cohort of newly diagnosed metastatic patients. Functional validation will employ glycosidase-treated EVs in organ-on-chip assays to demonstrate that ablation of specific glycan motifs redirects EV organ targeting. This approach would yield the first glycan-centric, pan-cancer liquid biopsy tool for predicting the destination of metastatic spread.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing a computational framework called GlycoTropNet that integrates tumor-cell glycosyltransferase and glycosidase expression profiles from TCGA and CPTAC pan-cancer datasets with organ-specific endothelial lectin receptor expression to predict glycan-mediated metastatic organotropism. The model will reconstruct the likely cell-surface glycome of each primary tumor using established glycosynthetic pathway logic and then compute interaction affinity scores between the inferred tumor glycome and organ-specific endothelial glycan-binding receptor landscapes curated from single-cell RNA-seq atlases of human vasculature. A graph neural network will learn from known tumor-to-metastatic-site pairs to identify glycosyltransferase expression motifs and lectin-glycan interaction axes that predict organ tropism. The framework will be validated against clinical metastatic outcomes from large institutional registries and the MSK-MET cohort. By bridging glycosynthetic enzyme expression to organ-specific vascular receptor landscapes in silico, GlycoTropNet would provide a novel, mechanistically grounded, pan-cancer organotropism predictor not previously attempted.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multiplexed lectin-based spatial glycomics approach using MALDI mass spectrometry imaging to map the N- and O-glycan landscapes of matched primary tumors and their organ-specific metastatic lesions across a pan-cancer tissue microarray cohort. By performing on-tissue PNGase F digestion and MALDI-MSI on hundreds of primary-metastasis pairs spanning multiple cancer types and metastatic organs, we will identify organ-destination-associated glycan structural motifs in primary tumors. These glycan imaging signatures will be distilled into a compact histopathology-compatible biomarker panel using supervised dimensionality reduction. The resulting classifier will be validated for its ability to predict metastatic destination from the glycan profile of primary tumor biopsies alone. Complementary lectin histochemistry on an independent validation cohort will enable a clinically deployable immunohistochemistry-equivalent assay. This study would be the first to leverage spatial glycomics at scale for organotropism prediction across cancer types.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a pan-cancer organotropism predictor based on sialylation and fucosylation signatures of circulating tumor cells captured from liquid biopsies. Using a microfluidic platform combining antibody-independent CTC capture with on-chip lectin staining for sialyl Lewis X, sialyl Lewis A, core fucose, alpha-2,6-sialic acid, and bisecting GlcNAc, we will quantitatively profile the glycan coat of individual CTCs from patients with diverse solid tumors and documented organ-specific metastases. Single-CTC glycan phenotyping will be analyzed by flow cytometry-analogous gating to classify glyco-phenotypic subpopulations correlating with liver, lung, bone, and brain tropism. A predictive model trained on these glyco-phenotypes will be tested prospectively in a validation cohort of patients at diagnosis to forecast the eventual site of first distant relapse. This approach uniquely combines single-cell glycan resolution on CTCs with pan-cancer organotropism prediction, offering a mechanistically informed and clinically accessible liquid biopsy strategy.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose building a biophysical glycan-lectin interactome model of organotropism by systematically measuring the binding kinetics between panels of recombinant organ-specific endothelial lectins (selectins, siglecs, galectins, C-type lectins varying by vascular bed) and synthetic glycan libraries representing tumor-associated glycan structures. Using biolayer interferometry and glycan microarray screening, we will construct an organ-by-glycan affinity matrix that quantifies the tropism potential of any given tumor glycan repertoire toward specific vascular beds. This affinity matrix will be integrated with tumor glycosyltransferase expression data from pan-cancer transcriptomic databases to infer each tumor's functional glycan presentation and compute a composite organotropism probability score. The model will be trained and validated using clinical datasets with paired primary tumor expression and metastatic site annotations. This biophysically grounded, bottom-up approach provides a novel mechanistic bridge between tumor glycobiology and metastatic destination prediction.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing a pan-cancer organotropism signature based on the glycoproteome of tumor-educated platelets obtained from routine blood draws. Platelets sequester and present tumor-derived glycoproteins on their surface, and their glycosylation patterns are altered upon interaction with tumor cells. Using lectin-enrichment coupled with quantitative glycoproteomics of platelets from patients with organ-specific metastases across multiple cancer types, we will identify metastatic-destination-specific glycoprotein and glycopeptide signatures. A random forest classifier trained on platelet glycoproteomic features will be tested for its ability to discriminate among patients destined for liver, lung, bone, and brain metastasis. Validation will be performed on a prospective cohort of newly diagnosed cancer patients followed longitudinally for metastatic events. This approach exploits the unique glycan-absorptive biology of platelets as sentinels of tumor glycan alterations and represents a novel, clinically practical glycobiology-based organotropism predictor.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a functional glycan-tropism assay using engineered organ-specific endothelial microenvironments on microfluidic chips to directly test the adhesion and transmigration preferences of patient-derived tumor cells or tumor organoid-shed EVs under physiological flow. Each channel of the chip will be lined with organ-specific endothelial cells (brain, liver, lung, bone marrow) expressing their native glycocalyx and lectin repertoire, verified by lectin staining. Tumor cells or EVs will be perfused through the multi-organ chip, and organ-specific adhesion events quantified via real-time imaging. By enzymatically modifying tumor cell surface glycans (neuraminidase, fucosidase, PNGase F) or blocking specific endothelial lectins before perfusion, we will dissect glycan-dependent mechanisms of organ-specific adhesion. The resulting functional adhesion profiles will be correlated with clinical metastatic outcomes to develop a functional glycan-based organotropism predictor. This platform would provide the first direct experimental readout linking tumor glycan presentation to organ-specific vascular adhesion in a patient-specific, pan-cancer context.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose mining the glycosyltransferase regulatory network as an organotropism predictor by constructing cancer-type-agnostic regulatory modules of co-expressed glycosyltransferases, their upstream transcription factors, and epigenetic regulators from pan-cancer multi-omic data. Using non-negative matrix factorization on combined transcriptomic, methylation, and chromatin accessibility data across TCGA cancers with known metastatic site annotations, we will identify latent glycosylation programs that correlate with tropism toward specific organs. These programs will be functionally validated by CRISPR perturbation of key glycosyltransferase module members in isogenic cancer cell lines, followed by experimental metastasis assays in mice to confirm altered organ tropism. A clinically deployable gene expression signature derived from the top-ranking glycosyltransferase modules will be validated in independent cohorts for prospective organotropism prediction. This regulatory network approach transcends single-gene glycosyltransferase analyses by capturing coordinated glycosylation programs that collectively determine the metastatic destination.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose SUMOylation-Recruiting Chimeras (SURCs), a bifunctional small-molecule platform that induces proximity between a target protein and the SUMO E2 conjugating enzyme Ubc9, thereby triggering poly-SUMOylation of the target and its subsequent recognition and ubiquitin-dependent degradation by the endogenous SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4. Unlike PROTACs that directly recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases, SURCs exploit an orthogonal post-translational modification cascade—SUMOylation followed by STUbL-mediated ubiquitination—as the initiating signal for proteasomal clearance. This two-step mechanism should confer enhanced selectivity, as degradation depends on both the induced SUMOylation event and the spatially restricted activity of RNF4 in nuclear and PML body compartments, making SURCs particularly suited for nuclear transcription factors and chromatin-associated oncoproteins that are poorly served by existing degraders. Synthetically, SURCs consist of a POI-binding ligand, a linker, and a small-molecule or peptidic Ubc9-recruiting moiety derived from known SUMO-consensus mimetics. We outline proof-of-concept studies targeting KRAS-G12D and MYC using SURCs, with validation by mass spectrometry-based SUMOylation profiling, RNF4 dependency assays, and xenograft efficacy models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Secretory Pathway Retro-Targeting Chimeras (SPRTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that divert plasma membrane or secreted proteins into the ER-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway by inducing proximity between a cell-surface protein of interest and a COPI-interacting retrieval motif mimic. Binding the target's extracellular domain, the SPRTAC co-opts COPI-mediated retrograde trafficking to redirect the target from the cell surface or Golgi back to the ER, where it encounters the SEL1L-HRD1 ERAD machinery and undergoes VCP/p97-mediated retrotranslocation and proteasomal degradation. This is mechanistically distinct from LYTACs and TransTACs, which route targets to lysosomes, and from PROTACs, which recruit cytosolic E3 ligases. SPRTACs are designed as cell-permeable peptidomimetic–small-molecule conjugates incorporating a KDEL-receptor-binding or KKXX-mimetic motif linked to a target-protein-binding warhead. This approach is especially suited for GPI-anchored proteins, immune checkpoint ligands, and other surface proteins that resist conventional lysosomal degradation. Feasibility rests on established knowledge of retrieval-signal chemistry and the demonstration that induced ubiquitination can trigger VCP-dependent ERAD for ER membrane proteins.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Condensate-Trapping Inactivation Chimeras (CTICs), bifunctional small molecules that functionally inactivate disease-relevant proteins by forcibly recruiting them into biomolecular condensates—specifically stress granules or p62 bodies—where they are sequestered from their normal functional compartment and eventually cleared by aggrephagy. One arm of the CTIC binds the target protein, while the other engages a core condensate scaffold such as G3BP1 (for stress granule recruitment) or the PB1 domain of p62 (for p62-body recruitment) via a validated small-molecule or peptide ligand. Unlike PROTACs or AUTACs, CTICs do not require direct recruitment of ubiquitin ligases or LC3; instead, they exploit the endogenous phase-separation-coupled autophagy pathway. Functional inactivation occurs both through physical sequestration in condensates and through subsequent autophagic clearance of the condensate contents. This approach is particularly suited for proteins with intrinsically disordered regions or multivalent interaction domains that are refractory to conventional degrader approaches. We detail proof-of-concept designs targeting oncogenic transcription factors such as EWS-FLI1, with readouts of condensate recruitment, functional inactivation, and tumor growth inhibition.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Exosomal Ejection Chimeras (EECs), bifunctional molecules that inactivate intracellular target proteins by rerouting them into extracellular vesicles through engagement of the ESCRT-associated sorting machinery. One moiety of the EEC binds the cytoplasmic target protein, while the other recruits Tsg101 or ALIX via short peptide motifs (PTAP or YPXnL) known to drive cargo loading into intraluminal vesicles of multivesicular bodies. Upon MVB fusion with the plasma membrane, the target protein is expelled from the cell as exosomal cargo, achieving functional depletion without proteasomal or lysosomal degradation. This mechanism is mechanistically orthogonal to all existing TPD modalities and is especially applicable to cytoplasmic signaling proteins and scaffolding factors that are difficult to degrade via conventional routes. The molecular design is a compact chimeric peptide-small molecule conjugate, synthetically tractable and compatible with cell-penetrating peptide delivery strategies. We outline validation experiments using proximity ligation assays for Tsg101 engagement, nanoparticle tracking analysis to quantify target enrichment in exosomes, and functional assays demonstrating intracellular target depletion in oncology models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy Targeting Chimeras (CMATACs), small-molecule bifunctional agents that hijack the chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) pathway by chemically inducing the display of a KFERQ-like motif on target proteins, thereby directing them for Hsc70 recognition, LAMP-2A-mediated lysosomal translocation, and intraluminal degradation. Unlike AUTACs and ATTECs, which engage macroautophagy through LC3 or S-guanylation, CMATACs exploit the mechanistically distinct CMA route, which selectively degrades individual soluble cytosolic proteins without autophagosome formation. The CMATAC molecule comprises a target-binding ligand linked to a synthetic KFERQ-mimetic peptide or peptidomimetic that is recognized by Hsc70, thereby creating a neo-CMA substrate. This platform is ideally suited for cytosolic monomeric proteins such as mutant p53, alpha-synuclein, or pathological tau variants, which are known to be regulated by CMA under physiological conditions. We describe the design, synthesis, and characterization of CMATAC prototypes, including demonstration of LAMP-2A-dependent degradation, selectivity over macroautophagy and the proteasome, and therapeutic efficacy in neurodegeneration models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Proximity-Induced Secretion Chimeras (PISCs), bifunctional molecules that functionally deplete intracellular target proteins by rerouting them into the conventional secretory pathway for extracellular expulsion. The PISC molecule links a target-protein-binding warhead to a synthetic signal-peptide mimetic or ER-insertion motif that co-opts the SRP-Sec61 translocation machinery, thereby redirecting cytosolic target proteins to the ER lumen during their next biosynthetic cycle. Once in the secretory pathway, the target is glycosylated, processed through the Golgi, and secreted, effectively depleting the intracellular pool without engaging proteasomes, lysosomes, or autophagosomes. This concept is mechanistically unique among TPD modalities and draws upon established signal-peptide engineering and the known plasticity of the Sec61 translocon. PISCs are best suited for soluble cytoplasmic proteins with pathological intracellular accumulation, such as mutant SOD1 or TDP-43 in ALS. Proof-of-concept experiments include demonstration of target secretion by ELISA of conditioned media, dependence on Sec61 and BFA-sensitive transport, and functional rescue in motor neuron disease models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose ISGylation-Recruiting Chimeras (IRCs), bifunctional small molecules that recruit the ISG15 conjugation machinery to a target protein, inducing its ISGylation and consequent functional inactivation, altered trafficking, or destabilization. ISGylation is an interferon-stimulated ubiquitin-like modification that can alter protein stability, protein-protein interactions, and subcellular localization, but has never been harnessed as a TPD effector mechanism. One arm of the IRC binds the target protein while the other recruits the ISG15 E3 ligase HERC5 or the E2 conjugase UbcH8 via a small-molecule or peptidomimetic ligand. Because ISGylation modifies newly translated proteins co-translationally, IRCs would preferentially target nascent copies of disease proteins, offering a kinetic selectivity advantage over conventional degraders that act post-translationally. This platform is particularly promising for viral proteins and immune-evasion factors where ISGylation has documented antiviral effects. We propose validation in SARS-CoV-2 and influenza infection models, measuring target ISGylation by immunoprecipitation, viral replication inhibition, and in vivo efficacy.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Induced Proximity Protease Chimeras (IPPCs), heterobifunctional molecules that recruit an endogenous cytoplasmic protease to a target protein, inducing its site-specific cleavage and consequent loss of function. Unlike all existing TPD modalities that rely on the proteasome, lysosome, or autophagy, IPPCs exploit the catalytic activity of calpains—calcium-dependent cysteine proteases that are constitutively expressed in the cytosol and activated by physiological calcium transients. One arm of the IPPC binds the target, while the other is a calpain-recruiting moiety derived from known calpain-substrate or calpain-activating peptide motifs. Proximity of calpain to the target protein induces proteolytic cleavage at permissive sites, generating non-functional fragments that are subsequently cleared by normal cellular housekeeping. This approach is particularly suited for large scaffolding proteins and multidomain signaling adaptors that possess flexible interdomain linkers susceptible to calpain cleavage. Proof-of-concept experiments target FAK and beta-catenin, with validation by cleavage-fragment western blotting, calpain-inhibitor rescue experiments, and functional readouts in cancer cell invasion and Wnt-pathway reporter assays.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a synthetic chromatin looping system termed "SonoLoop" that uses focused ultrasound to reversibly form and dissolve targeted chromatin loops in human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs), enabling on-demand osteogenic versus adipogenic gene expression switching. The system employs two orthogonal dCas9 proteins (dSpCas9 and dSaCas9) guided to an enhancer and a promoter, each fused to a split engineered calcineurin-responsive dimerization domain. Ultrasound activates endogenous Piezo1 mechanosensitive channels, triggering a calcium influx that activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates the engineered calcineurin-responsive split dimerization modules to enable their heterodimerization and thereby physically bridge the two genomic loci into a chromatin loop. Upon cessation of ultrasound, the calcium signal dissipates, calcineurin activity ceases, and kinase-mediated rephosphorylation dissolves the dimer interface, reversibly releasing the loop. This system is mechanistically distinct from optogenetic dimerizer-based approaches because loop formation is driven by an endogenous signaling cascade rather than direct photoreceptor-mediated protein-protein interaction, and it exploits a non-invasive, tissue-penetrant stimulus suitable for deep-tissue and in vivo applications in stem cell differentiation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose "ThermoLoop," a chromatin looping system that exploits focused ultrasound-induced mild hyperthermia to reversibly trigger thermoresponsive phase separation at targeted genomic loci, thereby forming or dissolving enhancer-promoter loops in human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) undergoing cardiomyocyte differentiation. Two orthogonal dCas9 variants are each fused to complementary engineered elastin-like polypeptide (ELP) domains with a tunable lower critical solution temperature set near 39-40 degrees Celsius; at physiological 37 degrees Celsius the ELPs remain soluble and the loci are uncoupled, but brief focused ultrasound raises the local temperature above the LCST, triggering ELP coacervation that physically bridges the two dCas9-bound loci into a loop. Upon ultrasound cessation, passive cooling dissolves the coacervate, reversing the loop. This design is fundamentally different from CRY2/CIBN or PhyB/PIF optogenetic dimerizers because looping is driven by a thermally controlled polymer phase transition rather than photoreceptor heterodimerization, offering a graded, dose-dependent response and deep-tissue compatibility without requiring genetic cofactors.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We describe "MagnetoLoop," a magnetically actuated chromatin looping system in which two genomic loci are tethered by orthogonal dCas9 proteins fused to anti-GFP nanobody and anti-mCherry nanobody, respectively, while GFP-ferritin and mCherry-ferritin fusion nanoparticles are co-expressed intracellularly. Under a radiofrequency alternating magnetic field, the superparamagnetic iron cores of both ferritin species generate local forces or torques that cluster the nanobody-bound ferritin particles, physically drawing the two dCas9-marked loci together into a chromatin loop. We target the beta-globin locus control region and HBB promoter in human erythroid progenitor cells derived from CD34-positive hematopoietic stem cells, aiming to reactivate fetal hemoglobin expression. Upon removal of the magnetic field, thermal fluctuations dissipate the weak magnetic clustering, and the loop dissolves. This mechanism is distinct from optogenetic dimerizer systems because it relies on physical magnetic force-mediated spatial colocalization of genomic anchors rather than light-induced protein-protein interaction, and it uses a fully tissue-penetrant stimulus compatible with in vivo therapeutic applications.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose "NIR-CohesinSwitch," a near-infrared light-controlled system that reversibly recruits or releases the cohesin loader NIPBL at specific genomic loci to induce or dissolve chromatin loops via the cell's endogenous loop extrusion machinery, tested in human neural progenitor cells for controlling neuronal differentiation genes. A dCas9 is guided to a desired cohesin loading site and fused to the QPAS1 domain of the near-infrared BphP1-QPAS1 optogenetic pair. A separate construct encodes the NIPBL HEAT-repeat domain fused to BphP1. Illumination at 740 nanometers converts BphP1 to its active state, recruiting NIPBL to the dCas9-bound locus, where it loads cohesin onto chromatin and initiates loop extrusion that forms or strengthens a loop anchored at the nearest CTCF boundary element. Illumination at 660 nanometers or dark reversion inactivates BphP1, releasing NIPBL and allowing WAPL-mediated cohesin unloading to dissolve the loop. This approach is mechanistically novel because it co-opts the native loop extrusion mechanism rather than directly tethering two distant loci, producing physiologically authentic loops with proper CTCF-dependent topology.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We introduce "AzoLoop," a fully reversible chemo-optogenetic chromatin looping platform that uses azobenzene-based photoswitchable molecular glues to bridge two dCas9-marked genomic loci in human T cells for inducible control of cytokine gene expression. Each of two orthogonal dCas9 proteins is fused to a small protein tag—HaloTag and eDHFR, respectively—and a cell-permeable diazocine-based photoswitchable molecular glue bearing both a HaloTag ligand and a trimethoprim moiety is added. Under green light the diazocine adopts its cis configuration, positioning the two ligand moieties to simultaneously engage both tags and physically bridge the two genomic loci into a loop; blue light isomerizes the switch to the trans state, separating the ligand ends and dissolving the loop. This system is differentiated from protein-based optogenetic dimerizers such as CRY2/CIBN because the dimerization event is mediated by a small synthetic molecule whose photoswitching kinetics are tunable through chemical modification, enabling multiple rapid on/off cycles without photobleaching or chromophore depletion. The T cell context enables demonstration of inducible IL2 enhancer-promoter looping and controlled cytokine secretion with therapeutic relevance.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose "SonoCondensate," an ultrasound-responsive synthetic condensate system for targeted chromatin looping in human hepatocytes, aimed at toggling metabolic gene expression programs. A dCas9 is targeted to a metabolic enhancer and fused to a synthetic intrinsically disordered region (IDR) engineered to have upper critical solution temperature (UCST) behavior with a transition near 40 degrees Celsius; a second dCas9 at the target promoter carries the same IDR. At 37 degrees Celsius the IDRs are phase-separated into a condensate that bridges the two loci, forming a chromatin loop. Focused ultrasound-induced mild local heating above 40 degrees Celsius dissolves the condensate and releases the loop; upon cooling the condensate re-forms. This inverted logic—where the default state is loop-on and ultrasound turns it off—provides a unique regulatory architecture not achievable with standard optogenetic activator systems and is especially suited for studying the consequences of loop dissolution at metabolic loci. The use of engineered UCST-IDRs rather than photoreceptor dimerizers represents a fundamentally new biophysical mechanism for stimulus-controlled chromatin architecture.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose "PhotoCTCF," a light-gated system that reversibly installs or removes synthetic CTCF boundary elements at targeted genomic positions to reshape topologically associating domain architecture and alter gene expression, demonstrated in human breast cancer cells at oncogene-harboring loci. A dCas9 is guided to a locus lacking a native CTCF site and fused to a LOV2-caged CTCF N-terminal domain; in the dark the LOV2 Jalpha helix sequesters the CTCF N-terminus, preventing cohesin interaction, while blue light illumination exposes the CTCF N-terminal cohesin-interaction surface, creating a de novo functional CTCF boundary that redirects ongoing cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and establishes new loop anchors. Dark reversion re-cages the CTCF domain within minutes, removing the synthetic boundary and dissolving the ectopic loops. This system is mechanistically distinct from dimerizer-based looping tools because it engineers a stimulus-responsive synthetic boundary element that reshapes loops through the native extrusion machinery, rather than physically tethering two specific loci together. Targeting the system to sites flanking oncogene-containing domains in breast cancer cells enables functional dissection of how TAD boundary perturbation contributes to oncogene misregulation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We describe "MagPhase," a magnetic field-responsive chromatin looping system that couples intracellular ferritin-mediated reactive oxygen species production to a redox-sensitive engineered protein dimerization module tethered to two dCas9-marked genomic loci in pancreatic beta cells, controlling insulin gene regulation. Each of two orthogonal dCas9 proteins is fused to one half of a split redox-sensitive coiled-coil whose heterodimerization is promoted by oxidation of engineered cysteine pairs and reversed by the cellular glutathione reductase system. Ferritin fusion proteins co-expressed in the cell produce a burst of localized ROS when exposed to a radiofrequency alternating magnetic field, oxidizing the coiled-coil cysteines and inducing dimerization that bridges the enhancer and promoter loci into a loop. Upon magnetic field removal, the endogenous reducing environment restores the reduced state and dissociates the dimer within minutes, dissolving the loop. This design is fundamentally different from optogenetic systems because it transduces a magnetic signal through a biochemical redox intermediate rather than through direct photon-driven conformational change, and it leverages the cell's own redox homeostasis for reversibility.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a stage-adaptive epigenetic therapeutic strategy that leverages CARM1 inhibition in combination with AMPK modulators to differentially control autophagy across cancer progression. In early-stage tumors where autophagy is tumor-suppressive, AMPK activators such as metformin would promote CARM1 nuclear translocation and TFEB-driven autophagy gene activation via H3R17me2a deposition, thereby reinforcing genomic integrity. Conversely, in advanced tumors where CARM1-TFEB-dependent autophagy fuels metabolic adaptation and therapy resistance, selective CARM1 inhibitors would block H3R17 dimethylation at CLEAR-element-containing promoters, suppressing pro-survival autophagic flux. This approach would be validated using patient-derived xenograft models stratified by tumor stage, monitoring autophagic flux, H3R17me2a ChIP-seq profiles, and TFEB/TFE3 nuclear localization. By anchoring the intervention in the AMPK-mTORC1-CARM1-TFEB signaling axis, this strategy directly addresses the context-dependent duality of autophagy and provides a clinically actionable framework for stage-specific epigenetic cancer therapy.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing PROTAC-based degraders targeting TFEB and TFE3 as a precision anticancer strategy to selectively ablate autophagy-lysosomal pathway activation in advanced cancers with constitutive MiT/TFE signaling. Unlike small-molecule inhibitors that block individual protein-protein interactions, PROTACs would eliminate the entire transcription factor pool, preventing compensatory activation of paralogous family members. Candidate PROTACs would be designed by conjugating MiT/TFE-binding warheads to E3 ligase ligands such as VHL or CRBN recruiters, and their efficacy would be assessed in FLCN-deficient renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma models where TFEB/TFE3 hyperactivation drives cytoprotective autophagy. Therapeutic specificity would be confirmed by monitoring CLEAR-element-driven gene expression, autophagic flux markers, and MHC-I surface restoration. This approach integrates autophagy's role in immune evasion, since TFEB-driven autophagy degrades MHC-I via NBR1, and thus PROTAC-mediated TFEB degradation could synergize with immune checkpoint blockade in immunotherapy-resistant tumors.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a combinatorial epigenetic strategy that pairs EZH2 inhibitors with selective autophagy modulators, stratified by p53 status, to exploit the interplay between H3K27me3-mediated gene silencing and autophagy regulation in cancer. In p53-wild-type tumors, EZH2 inhibition would de-repress BECN1 and key ATG genes silenced by promoter H3K27me3, restoring tumor-suppressive autophagy and activating p53-p21-mediated cell cycle arrest. In p53-mutant tumors, where EZH2 stabilizes gain-of-function p53 mRNA through a non-canonical mechanism, EZH2 degraders rather than catalytic inhibitors would eliminate both the methyltransferase and RNA-binding functions, while concurrent autophagy inhibition with hydroxychloroquine would block the pro-survival autophagy compensatory response. Validation would employ isogenic p53-WT and p53-null cell line panels, syngeneic mouse models, and patient-derived organoids, measuring H3K27me3 at ATG promoters, autophagic flux, and tumor regression.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose targeting the MYC-HDAC epigenetic rheostat to re-establish tumor-suppressive autophagy in MYC-amplified cancers. Overexpressed c-MYC recruits HDACs to silence MiT/TFE transcription factors and their downstream autophagy-lysosomal gene network, thereby disabling genomic quality control. Our strategy combines BET bromodomain inhibitors to reduce MYC transcription with selective class I HDAC inhibitors to restore histone acetylation at TFEB, TFE3, and core ATG gene promoters, re-engaging the autophagy-lysosomal pathway as a tumor suppressor. This dual approach would be tested in MYC-driven lymphomas and neuroblastomas using ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq to map chromatin accessibility changes at CLEAR elements and autophagy genes, alongside functional autophagy assays and tumor growth measurements. By specifically targeting the upstream epigenetic mechanism that shuts down protective autophagy rather than modulating autophagy directly, this strategy addresses the tumor-suppressive arm of autophagy's dual role and offers a mechanistically distinct therapeutic angle.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the METTL3-m6A-FOXO3 epitranscriptomic axis as a therapeutic target to overcome autophagy-mediated drug resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma and other solid tumors. METTL3 downregulation under hypoxic tumor microenvironment conditions reduces m6A methylation of FOXO3 mRNA, destabilizing FOXO3 transcripts and paradoxically activating cytoprotective autophagy through compensatory AMPK-dependent mechanisms that bypass normal FOXO3-mediated transcriptional control. We propose a combination of METTL3-stabilizing small molecules or mRNA-based METTL3 supplementation with AMPK-pathway-guided autophagy inhibitors to restore FOXO3-dependent apoptotic signaling while simultaneously blocking the alternative pro-survival autophagy route. Therapeutic efficacy would be evaluated in sorafenib-resistant HCC patient-derived xenograft models using m6A-seq to confirm epitranscriptomic restoration, single-cell RNA-seq to assess tumor heterogeneity, and combination index analyses to quantify synergistic drug interactions. This approach uniquely bridges epitranscriptomic regulation with autophagy-mediated resistance mechanisms.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a therapeutic strategy targeting the AMPK-EZH2-H3K27me3 axis to selectively reactivate autophagy-mediated tumor suppression in early-stage cancers harboring epigenetically silenced ATG genes. AMPK directly phosphorylates EZH2 at Thr311, reducing its H3K27me3-depositing activity and de-repressing TSC2 and key autophagy genes. In precancerous and early-stage tumor cells, pharmacological AMPK activation using next-generation direct activators combined with low-dose EZH2 catalytic inhibitors would synergistically remove the H3K27me3 repressive mark from autophagy-related gene promoters including BECN1, ULK1, and ATG9A, restoring their expression and tumor-suppressive autophagic function. Efficacy would be assessed in chemoprevention models using Apc-min mice and conditional KRAS-driven lung adenocarcinoma models at preneoplastic stages, with H3K27me3 CUT&Tag profiling at ATG loci and functional autophagy readouts. This epigenetic chemoprevention approach distinctly targets the tumor-suppressive window of autophagy before advanced-stage pro-tumorigenic reprogramming occurs.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a dual-targeting strategy combining EHMT2/G9a inhibitors with DNMT inhibitors to coordinately relieve the epigenetic silencing of autophagy genes in advanced cancers with high autophagic gene methylation burdens, thereby converting cytoprotective autophagy into autophagic cell death. EHMT2-mediated H3K9me2 deposition and DNMT-mediated DNA methylation cooperatively silence BECN1, BNIP3, and multiple ATG genes in invasive breast and colorectal cancers, maintaining a paradoxically low basal autophagy state that prevents autophagic cell death while other survival mechanisms remain active. Combined pharmacological inhibition of EHMT2 and DNMT using clinically available agents would massively de-repress the entire autophagy gene network, overwhelming the cancer cell with excessive autophagic flux and triggering autophagic cell death selectively in transformed cells. Validation would employ methylation-specific PCR and bisulfite sequencing of ATG promoters in matched normal-tumor tissue pairs, paired with dose-escalation studies in patient-derived organoids monitoring autophagic flux, cell viability, and SREBF2-dependent transcriptional activation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose an epigenetic immunotherapy approach in which selective inhibition of the TFEB-autophagy-lysosomal axis is combined with anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade to restore MHC class I surface expression and antitumor immunity in pancreatic and lung cancers. TFEB-driven autophagy promotes immune evasion by directing NBR1-dependent selective autophagy of MHC-I molecules to lysosomes, while simultaneously engaging CARM1-mediated H3R17me2a at autophagy gene promoters. We propose using pharmacological inhibitors of CARM1 arginine methyltransferase activity to disrupt the TFEB-CARM1 epigenetic coactivator complex, thereby reducing transcription of autophagy-lysosomal genes without completely eliminating basal autophagy, and restoring surface MHC-I levels. This epigenetic modulation would be combined with anti-PD-1 therapy and validated in syngeneic KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer models and orthotopic lung cancer models using flow cytometric quantification of surface MHC-I, CD8-plus T-cell infiltration assays, and tumor growth measurements. This strategy uniquely links epigenetic control of autophagy to tumor immunogenicity.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a cancer-stage-responsive epigenetic nanodelivery system that switches between autophagy-promoting and autophagy-inhibiting payloads depending on tumor microenvironment cues. Nanoparticles would be engineered with pH-responsive and hypoxia-responsive release mechanisms: at mildly acidic pH and moderate hypoxia characteristic of early lesions, they would release HDAC inhibitors that activate FOXO-dependent and TFEB-dependent autophagy gene expression to reinforce tumor-suppressive autophagy. Under the deeply hypoxic and acidic conditions of advanced tumors, the same particles would release autophagy inhibitors such as ULK1 inhibitors alongside CARM1 inhibitors to block the epigenetic activation of pro-survival autophagy genes. Proof-of-concept validation would use tumor spheroid models mimicking early and advanced microenvironments, followed by genetically engineered mouse models of stepwise tumorigenesis, with readouts including autophagic flux dynamics, histone mark profiling, and tumor growth kinetics. This approach directly addresses autophagy's dual role through a single adaptive delivery platform.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose leveraging single-cell multi-omics to identify and therapeutically target epigenetically defined cancer cell subpopulations that exhibit high autophagic flux and drive therapy resistance. Using paired single-cell ATAC-seq and RNA-seq, we would map chromatin accessibility at autophagy and lysosomal gene loci across heterogeneous tumor populations in treatment-naive and chemoresistant patient biopsies, identifying subclones with open chromatin at CLEAR elements and FOXO-binding motifs that correlate with elevated autophagy gene expression. Computational integration would nominate subpopulation-specific epigenetic vulnerabilities, such as dependency on BRD4-mediated super-enhancers at TFEB or CARM1 loci, which could be targeted using BET inhibitors or CARM1 degraders to selectively eliminate the autophagy-high resistant population. Functional validation would employ CRISPR-based epigenome editing of identified regulatory elements in patient-derived organoids, followed by assessment of chemosensitization and autophagic flux. This precision epigenetic approach addresses intratumoral heterogeneity in autophagy regulation, a dimension largely unexplored in current therapeutic strategies.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose targeting the HAT1-mediated H4K12 lactylation pathway in keratinocytes as a therapeutic strategy for obesity-associated psoriasis, where elevated lactate from metabolic overload amplifies a non-canonical IL-17 feed-forward loop that drives biologic resistance. In obesity, excessive glycolysis and lactate accumulation in the psoriatic skin microenvironment exacerbate histone lactylation, sustaining keratinocyte hyperproliferation independently of canonical chemokine signaling. We will design a topically deliverable small-molecule HAT1 inhibitor and test it in diet-induced obese mice subjected to imiquimod-induced psoriasis, measuring H4K12la levels, epidermal thickness, and IL-17A expression. Parallel experiments in a human keratinocyte-immune cell skin-on-chip model perfused with obesity-associated metabolites will assess whether HAT1 inhibition synergizes with anti-IL-17A biologics to restore therapeutic responsiveness. Readouts will include lactylation ChIP-seq, single-cell transcriptomics of epidermal and immune compartments, and barrier function assays. This approach directly addresses the metabolic memory that underpins biologic failure in obese psoriasis patients by intercepting the epigenetic node linking lactate metabolism to immune amplification.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose restoring PPARγ-positive skin-resident regulatory T cell function as an immune reprogramming strategy for obesity-associated psoriasis, based on the finding that obesity-derived long-chain free fatty acids induce lipotoxicity, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction selectively in this suppressive population. Our strategy employs topical nanoparticle delivery of the mitochondria-targeted antioxidant MitoQ combined with a PPARγ agonist to rescue skin Treg fitness in obese psoriatic skin. Using high-fat-diet-fed Foxp3-GFP reporter mice subjected to imiquimod challenge, we will quantify Treg survival, suppressive capacity, and IL-17A-producing γδ T cell expansion in treated versus untreated skin. Complementary skin-on-chip experiments incorporating human CD4 T cells, autologous keratinocytes, and palmitate-conditioned media will validate the translational mechanism. Primary endpoints include flow cytometric assessment of PPARγ-expressing Tregs, epidermal thickness, cytokine profiling, and PASI-equivalent scoring over an eight-week protocol. This approach uniquely addresses a root immunological deficit created by the obese metabolic environment rather than broadly suppressing effector cytokines.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose harnessing dermal white adipose tissue adipogenic reprogramming as an endogenous inflammation-resolving mechanism for obesity-associated psoriasis by pharmacologically accelerating PPARγ-dependent preadipocyte-to-adipocyte transition. Recent work shows that dermal preadipocytes initially amplify neutrophilic inflammation via CXCL1 and SAA3 but upon prolonged IL-1β exposure, PPARγ-driven differentiation generates anti-inflammatory lipid mediators that resolve disease. In obesity, this adipogenic resolution may be impaired by lipotoxic stress and inflammatory memory. We will administer a topical PPARγ modulator to diet-induced obese mice with imiquimod psoriasis, assessing neutrophil clearance kinetics, dermal adipocyte maturation by lineage tracing, and production of pro-resolving lipid mediators via lipidomics. An adipose-skin organ-on-chip incorporating PDGFRA-positive preadipocytes, keratinocytes, and immune cells will enable mechanistic dissection under obesity-mimicking metabolite conditions. This strategy reframes therapy from cytokine suppression to endogenous tissue resolution, leveraging dermal fat remodeling at the metabolic-epidermal interface.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose topical delivery of 4-octyl itaconate encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles to simultaneously reprogram dermal macrophages and keratinocytes in obesity-associated psoriasis. Itaconate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, activates Nrf2, and suppresses glycolysis-driven inflammatory polarization in macrophages, while in keratinocytes it can counteract HIF-1α-dependent Warburg-like metabolism that fuels IL-17 amplification. In obese psoriatic skin, where macrophage infiltration is increased and keratinocyte glycolysis is amplified by nutrient excess, dual-compartment metabolic reprogramming represents a novel therapeutic axis. We will test itaconate-loaded nanoparticles in high-fat-diet-fed mice challenged with imiquimod, assessing macrophage polarization by flow cytometry, keratinocyte glycolytic flux by Seahorse analysis, and disease severity by histopathology and cytokine measurement over six weeks. A psoriasis skin-on-chip with perfused macrophages and obesity-conditioned media will provide a human-relevant validation platform. This approach offers a metabolite-based, multi-cellular immune reprogramming strategy that is distinct from single-target biologics.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose an AMPK-activating gene therapy strategy using lipid nanoparticle-delivered mRNA encoding a constitutively active AMPKα2 subunit targeted to keratinocytes to correct obesity-driven mTOR hyperactivation and epigenetic inflammatory memory in psoriatic epidermis. Obesity suppresses epidermal AMPK, unleashing mTOR-dependent hyperproliferation, glycolytic rewiring, and pro-inflammatory gene programs that encode persistent metabolic memory and reduce biologic efficacy. Transient keratinocyte-targeted AMPKα2 mRNA delivery would restore metabolic sensing without systemic immunosuppression. We will evaluate this approach in K14-CreERT2 transgenic mice on a high-fat diet with imiquimod psoriasis, measuring epidermal thickness, mTOR pathway phosphorylation, histone acetylation patterns, and IL-17/IL-23 axis activation. Human organotypic skin equivalents cultured with hyperglycemic and hyperlipidemic media will serve as an in vitro complement. This gene therapy concept addresses the upstream metabolic rheostat that connects nutrient overload to epigenetic reprogramming at the metabolic-epidermal interface, offering a mechanistically distinct alternative to current psoriasis treatments.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that obesity-associated ferroptosis susceptibility in keratinocytes creates a self-amplifying inflammatory circuit at the metabolic-epidermal interface that can be therapeutically intercepted by combined FABP5 inhibition and GPX4 stabilization. Obese psoriatic skin exhibits elevated free fatty acids, FABP5-mediated lipid peroxidation, and suppressed GPX4, establishing ferroptosis-permissive niches that release DAMPs to activate IL-17, TNF-α, and IL-1β cascades. We will topically apply BMS-309403, a FABP inhibitor, with liproxstatin-1 in diet-induced obese mice subjected to imiquimod psoriasis, and monitor lipid peroxidation, neutrophil infiltration, keratinocyte death modality, and epidermal hyperplasia over four weeks. Parallel experiments in a human skin-on-chip perfused with palmitate-enriched media will validate the ferroptosis-inflammation axis. We will employ spatial lipidomics to map peroxidized phosphatidylethanolamine species at the dermal-epidermal junction. This combinatorial strategy targets the metabolic vulnerability of obese keratinocytes rather than downstream cytokines, potentially overcoming the biologic resistance observed in obese patients.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a dual-action therapeutic strategy coupling GLP-1 receptor agonism with topical epigenetic erasure of keratinocyte inflammatory memory to address obesity-associated psoriasis. While GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce systemic metabolic stress and adipose-derived inflammatory signals, they do not directly erase the epigenetic marks encoding persistent pro-inflammatory programs in keratinocytes established by prolonged metabolic overload. We will combine systemic semaglutide with topical application of a BET bromodomain inhibitor to simultaneously address systemic metabolic drivers and local epigenetic inflammatory memory in high-fat-diet-fed mice with imiquimod-induced psoriasis. Outcomes will include chromatin accessibility profiling of lesional keratinocytes by ATAC-seq, H3K27ac ChIP-seq to map active enhancer landscapes, as well as standard psoriasis endpoints including PASI scoring, epidermal thickness, and cytokine quantification. A multi-organ chip linking adipose and skin compartments will model the systemic-to-local therapeutic interplay. This combinatorial approach uniquely addresses both upstream metabolic reprogramming and downstream epigenetic memory simultaneously.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering an immunocompetent obesity-psoriasis skin-on-chip platform incorporating adipocyte-conditioned media, patient-derived keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and T cells to identify and validate sphingolipid rheostat modulators as novel therapeutics. Obesity disrupts the ceramide-to-sphingosine-1-phosphate balance in the epidermis, shifting the sphingolipid rheostat toward pro-inflammatory S1P signaling that enhances Th17 polarization and impairs barrier function. Using this chip, we will screen acid ceramidase inhibitors and S1P lyase activators that restore the ceramide-S1P equilibrium under obesity-mimicking conditions. Therapeutic candidates will be validated in vivo in high-fat-diet-fed mice with imiquimod psoriasis, measuring stratum corneum lipid composition by mass spectrometry imaging, T cell subset frequencies, and transepidermal water loss. The chip will enable real-time monitoring of immune cell migration, keratinocyte differentiation, and cytokine secretion in response to sphingolipid modulation. This approach targets the lipid-metabolic interface between epidermal barrier function and immune activation, a mechanism underexplored in obesity-associated psoriasis.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose boosting NAD+ bioavailability in psoriatic epidermis through topical delivery of nicotinamide mononucleotide to reactivate SIRT1-dependent anti-inflammatory and pro-differentiation programs that are suppressed by obesity-driven metabolic stress. Obesity depletes NAD+ pools through chronic PARP activation and increased CD38 expression, leading to SIRT1 downregulation in keratinocytes, which releases NF-κB from deacetylation-mediated repression and blocks terminal differentiation. By restoring the NAD+-SIRT1 axis specifically in the epidermis, this strategy would reprogram keratinocyte inflammatory transcription while promoting orderly differentiation, without systemic immunosuppression. We will deliver NMN via dissolving microneedle patches to high-fat-diet-fed mice with imiquimod psoriasis, measuring epidermal NAD+ levels, SIRT1 activity, NF-κB acetylation status, keratinocyte differentiation markers, and psoriasis severity indices over six weeks. A three-dimensional bioprinted skin model with human keratinocytes cultured in high-glucose, high-lipid media will validate the mechanism. This metabolite-based epigenetic strategy uniquely reconnects obesity-disrupted nutrient sensing to immune quiescence at the epidermal level.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multiplexed, chemically inducible chromatin loop engineering platform for controlling neuronal gene expression through programmable enhancer-promoter rewiring. The system deploys pairs of orthogonal dCas9 proteins (SpCas9 and SaCas9) each fused to complementary halves of a rapamycin-inducible FKBP-FRB dimerization module, guided to user-defined enhancer and promoter loci by arrayed sgRNAs. Unlike CLOuD9 and LADL, which demonstrated single-loop formation with modest transcriptional effects, our approach multiplexes four to six simultaneous loops at a neurogenic locus such as NEUROD1 or BDNF, titrating loop valency to achieve graded gene activation. Micro-C and nascent RNA-seq will establish the causal chain from de novo loop formation to transcriptional upregulation, and single-cell electrophysiology will link expression changes to neuronal firing properties. Crucially, by pairing dimerization with catalytically dead Cas9 lacking any epigenetic effector domains, the system bypasses histone modification and DNA methylation machinery entirely. This approach would provide the first dose-responsive, structure-only gene regulation toolkit in post-mitotic neurons.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose to control epithelial gene expression by engineering synthetic TAD boundaries using CRISPR-mediated insertion of oriented CTCF-binding site cassettes at defined genomic positions. Using base editing and prime editing to introduce convergently oriented CTCF motifs flanking a target gene locus—such as TGFBR2 or CDH1 in intestinal epithelial cells—we will create neo-boundaries that insulate the target from its native enhancers or redirect it toward alternative regulatory elements within the newly formed domain. Hi-C and Micro-C will verify de novo boundary formation and altered enhancer-promoter contact frequencies, while RNA-seq and Western blot will quantify transcriptional and protein-level changes. Functional assays for epithelial-mesenchymal transition, including wound healing and invasion assays, will establish the phenotypic consequences. Because the approach alters only the linear DNA sequence grammar read by endogenous CTCF and cohesin—without introducing exogenous epigenetic writers or erasers—it satisfies the constraint of independence from epigenetic machinery while demonstrating a permanent, heritable structural rewiring of gene regulation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a synthetic cohesin-loading station strategy to redirect loop extrusion and reshape enhancer-promoter contacts in neurons. A minimal NIPBL interaction domain will be fused to dCas9 and targeted to specific genomic sites near neuronal identity genes such as the clustered protocadherin locus, creating ectopic cohesin loading points that redirect the path of loop extrusion. By positioning synthetic loading stations asymmetrically relative to existing CTCF barriers, we will generate novel chromatin loops that bring previously insulated enhancers into contact with target promoters or sequester active promoters away from their endogenous enhancers. Micro-C will map the resulting structural changes, and single-cell RNA-seq will capture altered protocadherin isoform diversity as a transcriptional readout. The phenotypic consequence—altered dendritic self-avoidance patterning—will be assayed in cultured cortical neurons. This strategy fundamentally differs from prior dCas9-dimerization looping tools because it harnesses the cell's own loop extrusion motor rather than physically bridging two loci, enabling the formation of dynamically maintained, physiologically scaled loops.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose to control gene expression in epithelial cells by programmably relocating specific genomic loci between the nuclear lamina and the nuclear interior using an improved CRISPR-GO system. Using dCas9 fused to an inducible Emerin-targeting module, we will tether disease-relevant epithelial loci—such as TP63 or KRT14—to the nuclear periphery, disrupting their native TAD-level contacts and repositioning them into lamina-associated domains. Conversely, by targeting the same loci to nuclear speckles via SRRM2-fusion constructs, we will move them into transcriptionally active compartments. Time-resolved Micro-C, DamID, and RNA-seq will delineate the causal sequence from spatial repositioning to chromatin contact reorganization to transcriptional change. Phenotypic readouts will include keratinocyte differentiation markers and stratification in organotypic skin cultures. The novelty lies in systematically comparing lamina-tethering versus speckle-tethering of the same endogenous loci in the same cell type, establishing bidirectional, compartment-level control of gene expression that operates through nuclear spatial reorganization rather than through direct epigenetic modification.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose designing synthetic architectural RNA scaffolds—engineered non-coding RNAs containing tandem MS2 and PP7 aptamer arrays—to bridge two distant chromatin loci and form de novo enhancer-promoter loops without relying on endogenous architectural proteins or epigenetic machinery. Each scaffold RNA will carry aptamers that recruit MS2 coat protein fused to a dCas9 targeted to an enhancer and PP7 coat protein fused to a second orthogonal dCas9 targeted to a promoter, creating an RNA-bridged chromatin contact. We will apply this system in cortical neurons to rewire BDNF enhancer-promoter topology and in intestinal epithelial organoids to redirect WNT-responsive enhancers. 4C-seq and live-cell imaging of loop dynamics will confirm structural rewiring, while RT-qPCR and phenotypic assays—including neurite outgrowth for neurons and organoid crypt-villus patterning for epithelial cells—will complete the causal chain. The RNA scaffold is modular and degradable by RNase or antisense oligonucleotides, offering temporal reversibility superior to protein-dimerization approaches and enabling the study of loop dissolution kinetics on gene expression.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose an optogenetically controlled, locus-specific cohesin retention system to modulate chromatin loop size and gene expression in neurons. A dCas9 fusion carrying a photo-switchable anti-WAPL nanobody will be targeted to specific CTCF-anchored loop bases near activity-regulated neuronal genes such as FOS and ARC. Upon blue-light activation, the nanobody sequesters WAPL locally, preventing cohesin unloading at the targeted site and extending the loop to encompass additional enhancers or exclude the target promoter from its native regulatory domain. Dark reversal restores WAPL activity, enabling rapid loop retraction. This spatially restricted, light-inducible manipulation of cohesin dynamics contrasts with global WAPL depletion studies by providing single-locus resolution. Hi-C time courses under light-dark cycles will map dynamic loop restructuring, while calcium imaging and immediate-early gene expression will report functional consequences in cultured hippocampal neurons. The system operates entirely through structural protein dynamics without engaging histone-modifying or DNA methylation enzymes, offering a purely architectural mechanism of transcriptional control.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a combinatorial CTCF motif editing strategy using base editors to systematically invert, delete, or insert CTCF-binding sites around a defined epithelial gene regulatory locus—specifically the EGFR locus in lung epithelial cells—to construct a comprehensive map linking CTCF grammar to chromatin loop topology and gene output. By generating a library of isogenic cell lines each carrying distinct combinations of CTCF site orientations using adenine or cytosine base editors, we will quantify how motif polarity, spacing, and number at a single locus combinatorially control loop anchor usage and enhancer-promoter contact selection. Micro-C and CTCF ChIP-seq will report structural consequences, RNA-seq will capture transcriptional changes in EGFR and neighboring genes, and cell proliferation and EGFR signaling assays will establish phenotypic impact. This systematic, single-locus combinatorial perturbation goes beyond prior studies that altered one or two CTCF sites in isolation, providing the first comprehensive orientation-topology-expression transfer function at an endogenous disease-relevant locus in epithelial cells.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering phase-separation-competent but epigenetically inert synthetic condensate seeds at specific genomic loci to remodel local chromatin compartmentalization and thereby control gene expression. Using dCas9 fused to engineered intrinsically disordered regions derived from FUS or BRD4 but stripped of chromatin-reader and histone-binding domains, we will nucleate transcriptional condensates at target promoters in epithelial cells without recruiting endogenous histone-modifying activities. By targeting the condensate seeds to silent genes within B-compartment chromatin, we will test whether condensate-mediated A-compartment switching alone is sufficient to activate transcription and drive phenotypic changes such as epithelial differentiation. Complementary experiments will target active A-compartment genes with repressive condensate seeds bearing HP1-alpha's chromoshadow domain (but not its chromodomain, removing H3K9me3 dependence). Micro-C compartment analysis, single-cell RNA-seq, and differentiation assays will establish the causal chain from compartment switching to gene activation to phenotype. This approach disentangles phase-separation-driven compartmental reorganization from the histone code.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a dual-function synthetic insulator system that simultaneously creates a new TAD boundary and redirects an enhancer to a heterologous promoter in neurons. The system combines dCas9-mediated ectopic recruitment of the CTCF N-terminal domain plus two zinc fingers (a minimal cohesin-stalling module recently validated) at one genomic site with a CLOuD9-style dimerization bridge at a second site, deployed in the same cell at the same locus. Applied to the SCN1A locus implicated in Dravet syndrome, this dual system will erect a synthetic boundary between SCN1A and a neighboring enhancer while simultaneously looping a distal enhancer to the SCN1A promoter, thereby rewiring its regulatory inputs. Micro-C, allele-specific 4C-seq, and patch-clamp electrophysiology in iPSC-derived neurons will establish the causal chain from architectural change to sodium channel expression to neuronal excitability. The integrated boundary-plus-loop design represents a novel compound architecture-editing modality, addressing the limitation of single-tool approaches that can form loops but cannot simultaneously insulate against competing regulatory contacts.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a closed-loop wearable system that couples real-time respiratory phase detection with respiratory-gated olfactory micro-dosing to enhance emotion regulation in everyday settings. Nasal breathing entrains neural oscillations in limbic regions via the olfactory bulb, and specific odorants such as linalyl acetate can modulate amygdala–prefrontal circuits through olfactory receptor–mediated neurotrophic and serotonergic pathways. Our system uses a nasal airflow sensor embedded in a lightweight clip to detect inspiratory onset and then triggers a miniature microfluidic olfactometer to release brief pulses of anxiolytic odorant precisely at peak inhalation, when olfactory bulb–limbic coupling is maximal. By synchronizing olfactory stimulation to the respiratory cycle rather than delivering it continuously, the approach exploits the respiratory entrainment of cortical alpha oscillations and preBötzinger–locus coeruleus–prefrontal pathways to amplify both the neural and the autonomic calming effects beyond what either slow breathing guidance or passive aromatherapy achieves alone. A randomized crossover trial in adults with elevated subclinical anxiety will measure changes in state anxiety, frontal alpha asymmetry, and heart rate variability across a four-week daily-use protocol.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a dual-channel wearable that simultaneously delivers vibrotactile C-tactile afferent stimulation and transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation modulated by a shared closed-loop cardiac signal. C-tactile fibers in hairy skin project to the posterior insula and are selectively activated by gentle, slow-velocity mechanical stimuli resembling affective touch, while auricular vagus afferents modulate locus coeruleus–norepinephrine tone and amygdala reactivity. Our device integrates a mastoid piezoelectric actuator targeting C-tactile mechanoreceptors with an ear-clip electrode stimulating the auricular branch of the vagus nerve, both gated to fire during the cardiac diastolic phase when baroreceptor-mediated cortical inhibition is maximal. This triple convergence of affective touch, vagal afference, and cardiac-phase timing on insular–prefrontal circuits represents a mechanistically novel combination not previously investigated. We will evaluate the system in a sham-controlled trial measuring reductions in daily negative affect, skin conductance reactivity, and self-reported emotion regulation efficacy over six weeks in a non-clinical population with moderate trait anxiety.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing a wearable headband that combines transcranial photobiomodulation with phase-locked acoustic stimulation during overnight sleep to enhance next-day emotion regulation capacity. Transcranial near-infrared light targeting the prefrontal cortex upregulates mitochondrial cytochrome-c-oxidase activity, cerebral oxygenation, and neuroplasticity-related gene expression, while phase-locked auditory tones delivered at the up-phase of sleep slow oscillations boost slow-wave activity, spindle density, and parasympathetic tone. Although each modality has been studied in isolation, their combination during sleep is unexplored and may produce synergistic effects: enhanced prefrontal metabolic capacity could amplify the synaptic consolidation driven by acoustically boosted slow oscillations, strengthening the overnight recalibration of corticolimbic emotion circuits. The headband will use dry EEG electrodes for real-time slow-oscillation detection, integrated LEDs for 810 nm photobiomodulation, and bone-conduction speakers for acoustic delivery. A four-week randomized controlled trial in healthy adults will assess morning affect, cognitive reappraisal efficacy, and ecological momentary measures of daily anxiety and depressive symptoms.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a wearable interoceptive training system that uses heartbeat-contingent haptic feedback combined with adaptive AI-guided cognitive reappraisal prompts to improve everyday emotion regulation. Interoceptive accuracy, the ability to perceive internal bodily signals such as heartbeats, is linked to emotional awareness and regulation, yet most people have poor cardiac interoception. Our system delivers real-time heartbeat-synchronized vibrotactile pulses via a wrist-worn device to amplify cardiac interoceptive signals, while a companion application detects elevated heart rate and reduced heart rate variability to trigger brief, personalized cognitive reappraisal micro-exercises generated by a large language model fine-tuned on therapeutic reappraisal corpora. The novel mechanism lies in coupling bottom-up interoceptive enhancement with top-down reappraisal in a closed-loop architecture that bridges the predictive coding gap between visceral signals and prefrontal regulatory processes. A randomized controlled trial will compare this combined system against haptic-only, reappraisal-only, and waitlist conditions in non-clinical adults, measuring changes in interoceptive accuracy, daily affect, state anxiety, and frontal EEG asymmetry over eight weeks.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a technology that harnesses interpersonal physiological synchrony for emotion regulation by creating a wearable dyadic co-regulation platform. Two individuals, such as partners, close friends, or parent and child, each wear a wrist device that continuously monitors heart rate variability, electrodermal activity, and respiratory rate; when the system detects autonomic stress signatures in one member, it delivers subtle haptic breathing-pace cues to the partner calibrated to gently slow their respiration and increase their parasympathetic output, thereby facilitating physiological co-regulation through the well-established mechanism of interpersonal autonomic synchrony. Unlike individual biofeedback systems, this approach leverages the social regulation of emotion, wherein dyadic physiological alignment reduces arousal more effectively than solo self-regulation, and translates it into a technological intervention. We will test whether dyadic wearable co-regulation reduces daily anxiety, improves relationship satisfaction, and increases physiological synchrony relative to individual biofeedback and no-treatment controls in a twelve-week field trial with romantically partnered adults.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multimodal stochastic resonance platform for enhancing prefrontal emotion regulation circuits. Stochastic resonance, in which an optimal level of noise boosts subthreshold neural signal detection, has been demonstrated in perceptual domains but has never been applied to strengthen endogenous emotion regulation signals in the prefrontal cortex. Our system delivers individually calibrated low-intensity random noise simultaneously through three sensory channels: subliminal vibrotactile noise to the wrists, low-level auditory white noise via bone conduction, and faint stochastic visual luminance fluctuations through smart glasses. By converging multimodal noise on prefrontal and insular networks, we hypothesize that the composite stimulation will lower the threshold for detecting interoceptive and affective signals, thereby facilitating spontaneous reappraisal and attentional disengagement from negative stimuli. A within-subjects crossover design will compare active trimodal noise, unimodal noise, and sham conditions in healthy adults performing an emotion regulation task, measuring late positive potential amplitude, frontal theta power, and self-reported negative affect.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a non-invasive system that uses precision-timed, melanopic-spectrum micro-light pulses delivered through smart eyewear to modulate circadian-emotional coupling for everyday mood regulation. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells expressing melanopsin project not only to the suprachiasmatic nucleus for circadian entrainment but also directly to mood-regulating brain regions including the perihabenular nucleus, medial amygdala, and ventral prefrontal cortex. Unlike conventional bright light therapy, which uses prolonged static illumination, our approach delivers brief, algorithmically timed pulses of melanopsin-optimized light at moments personalized to each user's circadian phase, estimated from wearable actigraphy and pupillometry. The intermittent pulsing protocol exploits cone dark-adaptation dynamics to maximize ipRGC activation efficiency per photon, allowing mood-relevant circadian signaling at illuminance levels compatible with normal daily activities and without disrupting visual tasks. A chronotype-stratified randomized trial will evaluate whether four weeks of personalized melanopic micro-pulsing reduces depressive and anxiety symptoms and improves circadian regularity relative to constant-spectrum control lenses in a general population sample.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a closed-loop nocturnal emotion processing system that selectively modulates emotional memory consolidation during REM sleep using respiratory-gated auditory cues. During REM sleep, the brain reprocesses emotionally salient memories, and the efficiency of this affective depotentiation depends on prefrontal–amygdala coupling, which is rhythmically modulated by respiration. Our EEG-headband system detects REM epochs and monitors respiratory phase in real time; upon identifying expiratory phases when prefrontal inhibitory tone over the amygdala is elevated, it delivers soft, previously conditioned neutral auditory cues that were paired during waking hours with positive emotion regulation exercises. This respiratory-phase-specific targeted memory reactivation during REM represents a novel synthesis of three established but separately studied phenomena: targeted memory reactivation, REM-dependent emotional processing, and respiratory modulation of limbic circuits. A randomized sham-controlled home-use trial over six weeks will assess whether the intervention reduces next-day negative emotional reactivity, ruminative thinking, and trait anxiety in a general adult population with subclinical symptoms.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a cell-free chemoenzymatic strategy to install sialyl Lewis X (sLeX) tetrasaccharides on the surface glycoproteins of isolated extracellular vesicles (EVs), enabling them to home to E- and P-selectin-expressing cells at sites of inflammation. After EV isolation, endogenous heterogeneous N-glycans will be trimmed by endoglycosidase to the core GlcNAc, then a defined sLeX-bearing complex-type glycan oxazoline will be transferred en bloc using an engineered glycosynthase mutant. The resulting homogeneous sLeX-decorated EVs will be loaded with anti-inflammatory cargo (IL-10 mRNA or miR-146a) and evaluated for selective binding to TNF-α–activated endothelial cells under shear flow, with non-activated endothelium as a control. In vivo biodistribution and therapeutic efficacy will be assessed in a murine LPS-induced acute lung injury model, measuring EV accumulation at inflamed vasculature by near-infrared imaging and correlating it with reduced cytokine storm and tissue damage. This approach overcomes the low-affinity problem of free sLeX by presenting the glycan at high multivalent density on the natural EV membrane, a strategy not previously attempted via post-isolation chemoenzymatic remodeling on EVs.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose decorating isolated EVs with poly-N-acetyllactosamine (polyLacNAc) chains using sequential exogenous glycosyltransferase reactions to exploit the massive upregulation of galectin-3 in inflamed and fibrotic tissues. Galectin-3, a chimeric β-galactoside-binding lectin, is secreted by activated macrophages and deposited on the surface of damaged cells in inflammatory microenvironments, where it forms lattices that can capture polyLacNAc-bearing ligands with high avidity. Following EV isolation, native glycans will be enzymatically trimmed with neuraminidase and galactosidase, then rebuilt by iterative addition of GlcNAc and Gal using recombinant β1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase and β1,4-galactosyltransferase to generate extended polyLacNAc antennae. EVs will be loaded with NF-κB–inhibitory small molecules and tested for preferential uptake by galectin-3–positive cells in co-culture systems mimicking sterile liver injury. Therapeutic selectivity will be validated in a carbon tetrachloride hepatic fibrosis mouse model, comparing galectin-3–high inflamed regions with healthy tissue. This strategy uniquely targets pathological state rather than cell lineage because galectin-3 deposition is a universal hallmark of inflammation irrespective of the cell type affected.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose an EV glycoengineering platform in which isolated vesicles are post-synthetically modified with advanced glycation end-product (AGE)–mimetic glycans to target the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE), which is markedly upregulated on cells under oxidative stress, hyperglycemia, and chronic inflammation. After EV purification, amine groups on surface glycoproteins will be reacted with glycolaldehyde under mild, controlled conditions to generate Nε-carboxymethyllysine and related AGE epitopes that mimic natural RAGE ligands. The resulting AGE-decorated EVs will carry encapsulated anti-inflammatory siRNA against HMGB1 and will be assessed for RAGE-dependent uptake in TNF-α–stimulated versus quiescent endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes. In vivo validation will employ a diabetic wound healing model in which RAGE is highly expressed at injury sites, monitoring EV accumulation, wound closure, and inflammatory cytokine reduction.
