Donor chimerism is quantified from the fraction of donor-specific alleles, while tissue-of-origin deconvolution partitions the cfDNA into myeloid, lymphoid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic contributions, providing lineage-resolved engraftment data without cell sorting. Clonal diversity is inferred from the distribution of unique molecular identifiers at each informative locus and from the entropy of fragment length distributions reflecting distinct contributing cell populations. This entirely non-invasive approach requires only a standard blood draw and leverages existing targeted sequencing and methylation-aware library preparation workflows, with results obtainable within three days, supporting monthly longitudinal monitoring over one year post-HSCT.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose Mosaic-HSCT, a single-cell multi-omic platform adapted for post-transplant monitoring that simultaneously profiles donor-recipient informative SNPs, mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy, and surface protein expression in tens of thousands of individual cells per sample using a modified droplet-based microfluidic workflow. A custom amplicon panel targeting approximately 50 high-heterozygosity nuclear SNPs and the full mitochondrial genome is combined with an oligonucleotide-conjugated antibody panel recognizing lineage-defining surface antigens spanning all hematopoietic compartments including myeloid, lymphoid, erythroid, and megakaryocytic markers. At the single-cell level, nuclear SNPs determine donor versus recipient origin for each cell, surface proteins assign lineage identity without prior sorting, and mitochondrial heteroplasmic variants serve as endogenous clonal barcodes linking cells of shared stem cell origin. Clonal diversity is computed as the number and distribution of distinct mtDNA clonal groups within the donor compartment across each lineage. The platform runs on commercially available single-cell DNA-sequencing instruments with two-to-three-day turnaround and moderate per-sample cost, and we propose validation through a longitudinal cohort study with monthly sampling for one year post-HSCT.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose PhyloGraft, a method that performs low-pass whole genome sequencing on small pools of FACS-sorted hematopoietic lineage subsets to detect somatic single-nucleotide variants acquired during donor hematopoietic stem cell life history, then uses these variants as natural phylogenetic barcodes to reconstruct the clonal architecture of the reconstituting graft. From a single peripheral blood draw, six lineage fractions are sorted and sequenced at five-to-ten-fold genome coverage, with donor pre-transplant DNA serving as the germline reference. Shared somatic variants across lineage fractions confirm multilineage engraftment from individual stem cell clones, while variants unique to specific lineage pools reveal lineage-restricted contributions. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree is constructed at each longitudinal time point, and polyclonal diversity is quantified by the number of distinct founding branches and their relative contributions. Unlike retroviral integration site analysis, this approach requires no genetic modification and unlike targeted panels, it provides genome-wide resolution for clone discrimination. The method is designed for monthly monitoring with clinical-grade sequencing infrastructure and validated against parallel STR chimerism assessment in a 40-patient prospective cohort over one year.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering a gut-resident synthetic microbial consortium (based on Bacteroides and E. coli Nissle 1917 chassis) that autonomously senses the post-dieting metabolic state via a leptin-responsive transcriptional circuit and secretes a blood-brain barrier-permeable peptidomimetic agonist of the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R) directly into the portal circulation. Unlike canonical satiety peptides, this engineered agonist would be a protease-resistant cyclic peptide that bypasses classical vagal afferent pathways and instead reaches arcuate POMC neurons hematogenously through the median eminence's fenestrated capillaries. The synthetic circuit would incorporate a bistable genetic switch calibrated to circulating leptin levels: when leptin falls below a diet-induced threshold, the bacteria constitutively produce the MC4R agonist, restoring melanocortin tone and directly opposing AgRP/NPY potentiation. The system's durability stems from the self-replicating bacterial chassis, which maintains tonic agonist production for as long as leptin remains suppressed, thus circumventing central desensitization by providing a sustained, non-pulsatile signal operating at a receptor locus downstream of the desensitized leptin receptor itself. Feasibility is supported by existing synthetic biology toolkits for gut commensals and the demonstrated capacity of portal-delivered peptides to reach hypothalamic targets.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the recently identified portal vein–spinal ascending pathway to Gcg-positive neurons of the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract as a vagus-independent conduit for anti-hunger signaling after diet-induced weight loss. Specifically, we will engineer enteroendocrine L-cells via adeno-associated virus-mediated transduction to constitutively express and secrete a synthetic mu-opioid receptor antagonist peptide into the portal venous milieu, where spinal afferent terminals bearing opioid receptors relay nutrient-related signals to the brainstem and hypothalamus. This strategy is grounded in evidence that portal mu-opioid antagonism triggers intestinal gluconeogenesis and activates satiety-promoting brain circuits through spinal rather than vagal routes, providing a signaling modality entirely distinct from GLP-1, PYY, CCK, or vagal afferent activation. The durability of the signal is ensured by the continuous self-renewal of L-cells from intestinal stem cells that incorporate the transgene, while the magnitude is calibrated by coupling transgene expression to a nutrient-sensing promoter that increases output during caloric restriction. This approach directly counteracts the PVHTRH-to-AgRP hunger synapse amplification by tonically engaging brainstem anorexigenic circuits that project to the paraventricular hypothalamus.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that gut-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), engineered to carry specific microRNA cargo, can be deployed as a novel humoral signaling modality to epigenetically reprogram hypothalamic feeding circuits following diet-induced weight loss. Enteroendocrine cells or intestinal epithelial cells will be transduced in vivo using lipid nanoparticle-delivered mRNA encoding a chimeric protein that loads selected miRNAs—targeting AgRP promoter-associated transcripts or NMDA receptor subunit mRNAs—into exosomes bearing transferrin receptor ligands for blood-brain barrier transcytosis. These gut-origin EVs would constitute a chronic, meal-entrained epigenetic signal fundamentally different from peptide hormones or neural impulses, acting to suppress AgRP transcription and reduce NMDAR-dependent synaptic potentiation at PVHTRH-to-AgRP synapses. Because miRNA-mediated gene silencing is catalytic and operates at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level, even low-titer vesicle delivery can produce durable suppression of hunger circuit gain, circumventing the rapid desensitization that plagues receptor-mediated satiety signals. Feasibility rests on demonstrated BBB crossing by gut-derived EVs, established miRNA packaging technologies, and the known role of H3K9 methylation at the AgRP promoter in regulating hunger-gene expression.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose harnessing enteric viscerofugal neurons—a class of ENS neurons that uniquely project axons out of the gut wall to prevertebral sympathetic ganglia—as a non-vagal neural conduit for transmitting a synthetic satiety signal from the gut to the central nervous system. These neurons, recently shown to generate synchronized 2-Hz burst firing patterns that activate sympathetic neurons, will be genetically targeted using retrograde viral vectors injected into the inferior mesenteric ganglion to express a designer receptor (DREADD) activated by a gut-lumen-stable, orally bioavailable synthetic ligand. Upon meal ingestion, the ligand activates viscerofugal neurons, which relay excitatory cholinergic signals through prevertebral ganglia to spinal intermediolateral column neurons and subsequently to hypothalamic circuits regulating energy balance. This pathway bypasses classical vagal afferents entirely, exploiting the established but therapeutically untapped sympathetic reflex arc. Tonic activation of this circuit following diet-induced weight loss would engage sympathetic outflow patterns that increase energy expenditure and suppress rebound hyperphagia, counteracting the AgRP potentiation that drives weight regain.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that enteric glial cells, which function as astrocyte-like integrators within the ENS and form direct contacts with both enteroendocrine neuropod cells and extrinsic nerve terminals, can be reprogrammed to serve as autonomous satiety-signal amplifiers that counteract post-dieting weight regain. Using AAV vectors with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) promoters delivered via colonic submucosal injection, enteric glia will be engineered to express a chimeric receptor that senses declining leptin (via a leptin-binding ectodomain) and, upon activation, releases brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and the atypical cytokine ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF)—both of which act on hypothalamic neurons through gp130/TrkB signaling pathways distinct from canonical satiety peptide receptors. CNTF is known to reduce body weight in humans without inducing the desensitization observed with leptin, and BDNF potentiates POMC neuron activity independently of the leptin-STAT3 axis. Enteric glia continuously sense their microenvironment and have privileged access to both the portal bloodstream and spinal afferent terminals, enabling dual-route humoral and neural signal propagation to hypothalamic feeding centers. This approach transforms a quiescent cell population into a sustained, desensitization-resistant source of anorexigenic neurotrophins calibrated to the energy-deficit state.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering a population of intestinal enteroendocrine neuropod cells to release the unconventional neurotransmitter D-serine, an NMDA receptor co-agonist, as a strategy to directly modulate the NMDAR-dependent synaptic plasticity at PVHTRH-to-AgRP synapses that drives weight regain after dieting. Neuropod cells, which already possess synaptic vesicle release machinery and form glutamatergic connections with peripheral neurons, will be transduced using intestinal organoid-based cell therapy to express serine racemase under a calorie-sensing promoter. D-serine, released into the portal circulation and capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier, would tonically occupy the glycine-binding site on GluN1 subunits of NMDARs on AgRP neurons. Paradoxically, sustained low-level D-serine exposure is predicted to produce NMDAR desensitization through receptor internalization, thereby directly blunting the NMDAR-dependent long-term potentiation at the hunger synapse. This mechanism inverts the conventional satiety paradigm: rather than activating anorexigenic receptors, it attenuates the excitatory plasticity mechanism itself. The approach is grounded in the established pharmacology of NMDAR co-agonist site modulation and the emerging capacity for neuropod cell transplantation from intestinal organoids.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a synthetic immunological relay system in which gut mucosal immune cells are co-opted to generate a durable anti-orexigenic cytokine signal following diet-induced weight loss, operating through the gut-associated lymphoid tissue rather than through canonical satiety peptides or vagal afferents. Engineered probiotic bacteria will constitutively present a neoantigen peptide to intestinal dendritic cells, inducing a controlled, low-grade Th1-polarized mucosal immune response that tonically produces IL-6 and CNTF-family cytokines acting on hypothalamic neurons through the circumventricular organs. IL-6 signaling through gp130-JAK-STAT3 in POMC neurons enhances melanocortin output independently of leptin, while simultaneously activating SOCS3 in AgRP neurons to dampen their orexigenic drive. The immunological memory inherent to this approach provides built-in durability: once mucosal T-cell clones are expanded, they persist for months, generating a sustained cytokine tone that resists the rapid tachyphylaxis affecting peptide hormone signaling. Biocontainment is ensured through kill-switch genetic circuits in the probiotic chassis, and signal magnitude is tunable by adjusting bacterial dosing. This immune-to-brain axis represents a novel modality that leverages the gut's largest organ system—its immune compartment—as an intermediary for central appetite regulation.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that tonic modulation of hepatic portal vein glucose sensing, achieved by engineering jejunal enterocytes to constitutively express intestinal gluconeogenesis enzymes (glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) at supraphysiological levels, can generate a sustained anorexigenic portal glucose signal that counteracts hypothalamic hunger-circuit adaptations after dieting. Intestinal gluconeogenesis produces glucose released into the portal vein, which is sensed by portal SGLT3-expressing spinal afferent neurons—a pathway demonstrated to be vagotomy-resistant and distinct from canonical vagal or peptidergic satiety mechanisms. The resulting spinal afferent activation projects to the parabrachial nucleus and hypothalamus, suppressing AgRP neuron activity and promoting POMC-mediated anorexia through a nutrient-sensing rather than hormonal modality. AAV-mediated transduction of jejunal epithelium with these enzymes under a constitutive intestinal promoter would ensure continuous portal glucose elevation independent of dietary protein or fiber intake, effectively mimicking the satiety-promoting effects of high-protein diets. Because this signal operates through a metabolic rather than receptor-ligand mechanism, it is inherently resistant to the receptor desensitization that undermines peptide-based therapies, and its magnitude scales with the transduced cell mass, providing a therapeutically adjustable and durable intervention.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multi-axis recovery protocol termed Compressed Restorative Sleep Architecture Enhancement (CRSAE), which uses closed-loop transcranial electrical stimulation with temporal interference (TES-TI) during a restricted sleep window to amplify slow-wave activity density and spindle-slow oscillation coupling, thereby accelerating synaptic renormalization, glymphatic clearance, and autonomic rebalancing within truncated sleep. The approach targets ventromedial prefrontal slow-wave generators at 0.75–1 Hz during NREM sleep to boost delta power per unit time, while simultaneously monitoring heart rate variability as a real-time autonomic feedback signal. We hypothesize that intensified slow-wave density will compress the homeostatic dissipation of sleep pressure — measured by adenosine clearance kinetics, cortical slope recovery, and Process S modeling — into fewer hours, while concurrently restoring parasympathetic tone, suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokine elevation, and normalizing insulin sensitivity. The study would employ a randomized crossover design comparing 5-hour sleep with TES-TI versus 5-hour sham-sleep and 8-hour normal sleep, with comprehensive multi-system biomarker panels (neurocognitive psychomotor vigilance, continuous glucose monitoring, circulating IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and spectral HRV) assessed over five consecutive restricted-sleep nights. This integrative neuromodulation-during-sleep strategy differs from prior single-domain stimulation studies by explicitly testing whether compressed SWA can produce system-wide recovery equivalence.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the recently discovered norepinephrine-vasomotion-CSF pumping axis to enhance glymphatic brain clearance within restricted sleep periods. During NREM sleep, oscillatory norepinephrine release from the locus coeruleus drives slow vasomotion that acts as a perivascular pump for cerebrospinal fluid influx and metabolic waste efflux. Our strategy uses closed-loop transcutaneous focused ultrasound stimulation targeted to cerebral arterioles, phase-locked to endogenous slow-wave down-states detected by wearable EEG, to amplify vasomotor oscillations during brief sleep bouts without extending total sleep time. We predict this will enhance clearance of adenosine, amyloid-beta, and other neurotoxic metabolites that accumulate during extended wakefulness, thereby reducing neurocognitive impairment and the secondary neuroimmune activation triggered by waste accumulation. A feasibility trial would measure CSF tracer dynamics via intrathecal gadolinium MRI, salivary and serum inflammatory markers, continuous glucose monitoring, and heart rate variability before and after five nights of restricted sleep with active versus sham ultrasound augmentation. This approach is novel in that it directly targets the physiological pump mechanism of brain clearance rather than indirectly modulating neural oscillations.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a waking-state vagally-mediated multi-system restoration protocol that combines transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) with phase-locked slow breathing at 0.1 Hz during structured daytime sessions to simultaneously address autonomic, immune, metabolic, and secondary neurocognitive impairments from sleep restriction. Chronic sleep loss drives sympathovagal imbalance and cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway withdrawal, elevating IL-6, TNF-alpha, and C-reactive protein while impairing insulin sensitivity and prefrontal cognitive function. We hypothesize that optimized taVNS parameters (25 Hz, 250 microsecond pulse width, intensity titrated to detection threshold) combined with resonance-frequency breathing will synergistically restore vagal tone, re-engage the cholinergic anti-inflammatory reflex, lower glycolytic flux and thus lactate-driven histone lactylation in neutrophils, and improve prefrontal cortical function via locus coeruleus modulation. The proposed study would randomly assign sleep-restricted adults to active taVNS plus paced breathing, taVNS alone, breathing alone, or sham during four 20-minute daily sessions across a five-day sleep restriction protocol, measuring HRV spectral indices, circulating cytokines, neutrophil H3K18 lactylation levels, glucose tolerance, and working memory performance. This is distinctive in targeting the vagal-immune-metabolic nexus as a unified pathway rather than treating each deficit independently.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that circadian-aligned early time-restricted eating (eTRE, 8-hour morning-centered feeding window) can selectively compensate for the metabolic, immune, and autonomic disruptions of chronic sleep restriction by restoring peripheral clock gene oscillations that are normally entrained by sleep-coupled fasting. Sleep deprivation disrupts peripheral circadian rhythms in liver, adipose tissue, and immune cells, leading to insulin resistance, inflammatory cytokine dysregulation, and sympathetic overdrive. Early TRE realigns feeding-fasting cycles with the central clock, re-establishing diurnal oscillations in DBP transcription factor activity, beta-cell insulin sensitivity, and cortisol rhythmicity, even when sleep is curtailed. We propose a randomized controlled trial in which adults undergo two weeks of sleep restriction (5 hours per night) while randomized to eTRE versus ad libitum eating, with comprehensive assessment of glucose clamp-derived insulin sensitivity, 24-hour cytokine profiles, clock gene expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, and autonomic function via continuous HRV and blood pressure monitoring. Neurocognitive outcomes (psychomotor vigilance, working memory) would be co-primary endpoints to determine whether metabolic-immune-autonomic restoration indirectly supports cognitive resilience. The novelty lies in framing TRE not merely as a metabolic intervention but as a multi-system sleep-loss countermeasure operating through peripheral circadian re-entrainment.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a pharmacological strategy to intercept the lactate-histone lactylation-RORalpha inflammatory axis that was recently shown to mediate sleep-deprivation-induced neutrophilic inflammation across species. Sleep loss increases glycolytic flux, elevates tissue lactate, enhances H3K18 lactylation at the RORalpha promoter, and triggers a systemic cytokine storm with downstream autonomic and metabolic consequences. We hypothesize that targeted suppression of this axis using low-dose dichloroacetate (DCA), a pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase inhibitor that redirects pyruvate from lactate production into mitochondrial oxidation, will attenuate immune dysregulation and its cascading effects on insulin sensitivity and sympathovagal balance during sleep restriction. A controlled study would administer oral DCA at sub-therapeutic oncology doses to sleep-restricted healthy adults and assess neutrophil lactylation levels, circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines, continuous glucose monitoring, HRV, and neurocognitive performance over a five-day protocol. By targeting the mechanistic root — metabolic reprogramming of immune cells — rather than downstream symptoms, this approach could prevent the immune-metabolic cascade while preserving sleep-pressure-dependent neurocognitive recovery mechanisms. This represents a novel application of metabolic-epigenetic targeting to the sleep deprivation context.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose using structured high-intensity interval exercise (HIIE) timed to the late afternoon circadian window as a multi-system countermeasure for sleep-restriction-induced homeostatic deficits, leveraging exercise's unique capacity to simultaneously activate glymphatic clearance-promoting mechanisms, restore autonomic balance, modulate immune function, and enhance insulin sensitivity. Acute exercise transiently increases norepinephrine oscillations and cerebral blood flow dynamics that parallel sleep-dependent glymphatic pumping, while also elevating anti-inflammatory myokine release (IL-6 from muscle acts in an anti-inflammatory paracrine mode distinct from pathological IL-6 elevation), enhancing GLUT4 translocation and insulin-independent glucose uptake, and acutely increasing parasympathetic reactivation during post-exercise recovery. We hypothesize that a precisely timed 20-minute HIIE session during the late-afternoon circadian peak of cortisol decline can partially recapitulate the homeostatic restoration functions of lost sleep across all four axes. The proposed crossover study would compare five days of sleep restriction (5 hours per night) with and without daily afternoon HIIE, measuring pre- and post-intervention neurocognitive function, continuous glucose monitoring, 24-hour inflammatory cytokine profiles, and ambulatory HRV. The innovation is in providing mechanistic evidence for exercise as a genuine multi-axis sleep-loss compensation strategy rather than a general wellness adjunct.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing a wearable closed-loop acoustic stimulation system optimized for ultra-short nap opportunities (20-minute naps, twice daily) that uses real-time EEG phase detection to precisely entrain slow oscillation-spindle complexes during brief daytime NREM episodes, thereby maximizing the restorative yield of minimal sleep periods. Prior work demonstrates that acoustic stimuli time-locked to slow-wave up-states can boost slow oscillatory power and spindle coupling, processes that mediate synaptic downscaling and memory consolidation, but this has not been tested as a compensatory strategy under chronic sleep restriction using optimized ultra-short nap protocols. We hypothesize that acoustically enhanced brief naps will produce synaptic renormalization disproportionate to nap duration, as measured by TMS-evoked cortical slope as a biomarker of net synaptic strength, while the increased slow-wave density will secondarily activate glymphatic clearance and promote parasympathetic recovery during these windows. A controlled trial would compare sleep-restricted participants (5 hours nocturnal sleep) receiving acoustically augmented naps versus sham-naps versus no naps, with assessment of cortical excitability, psychomotor vigilance, serum inflammatory markers, insulin sensitivity, and cardiac autonomic function. This approach is unique in targeting the quality rather than quantity of supplemental sleep as the intervention variable.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a combinatorial strategy that pairs daytime exposure to non-visual 480 nm enriched blue light at circadian-phase-appropriate timing with evening low-dose melatonin administration to restore the amplitude and phase coherence of central and peripheral circadian oscillators disrupted by chronic sleep restriction, thereby reinstating rhythmic control over immune, metabolic, and autonomic function. Sleep deprivation flattens cortisol and melatonin amplitude, desynchronizes core clock gene expression in peripheral tissues, and uncouples autonomic circadian modulation, resulting in nocturnal sympathetic dominance, daytime insulin resistance, and loss of the normal nocturnal anti-inflammatory milieu. We hypothesize that reinforced circadian amplitude through calibrated blue light exposure during the biological morning and exogenous melatonin at the dim-light melatonin onset will restore clock gene oscillation amplitude (BMAL1, PER2, CRY1) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells, normalize the diurnal cortisol curve, re-establish the nocturnal dominance of parasympathetic tone, and improve glucose homeostasis even under a 5-hour sleep schedule. The proposed crossover study would assess circadian biomarkers, inflammatory profiles, continuous glucose monitoring, and cognitive performance over two weeks of sleep restriction with versus without the light-melatonin protocol. This differs from simple bright-light therapy by integrating peripheral clock gene measurements as mechanistic endpoints and explicitly targeting multi-system restoration rather than alertness alone.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multi-axis organ-on-a-chip platform that integrates iPSC-derived sensory neurons, primary keratinocytes, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and key immune populations (Th2 cells, dendritic cells, mast cells) into a vascularized, innervated full-thickness skin equivalent under microfluidic perfusion. The system will be colonized with defined commensal and dysbiotic microbial communities (Staphylococcus epidermidis vs. S. aureus-dominated consortia) to simultaneously model all four AD pathophysiological domains. ScRNA-seq of dissociated chip compartments at sequential time points will map cell-state transitions, ligand-receptor crosstalk between sensory neurons and immune cells, barrier protein expression dynamics, and microbiome-driven transcriptional reprogramming. Computational inference of gene-regulatory networks will identify convergent signaling nodes across the barrier, immune, neural, and microbial axes. Candidate node inhibitors will be screened on-chip using combinatorial drug dosing via the microfluidic channels, with therapeutic efficacy assessed through barrier integrity metrics, cytokine secretion, neurite retraction, and microbial composition shifts. This unified platform will yield mechanistic insight into AD axis crosstalk and actionable therapeutic targets with translational relevance.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose to generate a conditional, keratinocyte-specific filaggrin-knockout mouse crossed with a TRPV1-Cre-tdTomato sensory neuron reporter line, creating a dual-transgenic model that simultaneously captures skin barrier dysfunction and enables visualization and functional interrogation of pruriceptive nerve fibers in AD-affected skin. Mice will be raised under gnotobiotic conditions and colonized with defined microbial consortia representing healthy or AD-associated dysbiotic communities to model microbiome-driven disease modulation. At disease onset and progression stages, lesional and non-lesional skin, draining lymph nodes, and dorsal root ganglia will be subjected to multiplexed scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics to map immune cell heterogeneity, neuro-immune signaling molecules, barrier gene programs, and microbiome-responsive pathways with spatial resolution. Network-level integration of these datasets will identify druggable crosstalk hubs linking barrier defects to neurogenic inflammation and microbial dysbiosis. Candidate therapeutics targeting these hubs, including neuropeptide receptor antagonists and microbiome-modulating postbiotics, will be tested in the same model using disease severity scoring, itch behavior analysis, and scRNA-seq-based pharmacodynamic readouts.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We will develop a modular skin-on-a-chip platform in which CRISPR-engineered FLG-knockdown keratinocytes, patient-derived Th2 and Th17 cells, iPSC-derived sensory neurons, and live skin-relevant microbial communities are compartmentalized yet fluidically connected. This design enables orthogonal perturbation of each AD axis independently or in combination, allowing systematic dissection of causality among barrier failure, immune polarization, neurogenic signaling, and microbial dysbiosis. After controlled perturbations such as S. aureus superantigen challenge, IL-4/IL-13 stimulation, or capsaicin-driven neuronal activation, cells from each compartment will be harvested for droplet-based scRNA-seq to characterize transcriptional responses at single-cell resolution. CellChat and NicheNet analyses will reconstruct inter-compartment communication networks and reveal how perturbation of one axis propagates to others. Identified convergence pathways, such as TSLP-IL-31 neuro-immune loops or microbiome-mediated aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling, will be pharmacologically targeted using small molecules, and therapeutic efficacy will be quantified by transepithelial resistance, cytokine profiling, and neuronal calcium imaging.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a longitudinal scRNA-seq atlas of the MC903-induced AD mouse model enhanced with dorsal root ganglion sampling and concurrent 16S/ITS metagenomics of lesional skin microbiota at seven time points spanning disease initiation, acute flare, chronicity, and spontaneous resolution. By profiling skin, draining lymph nodes, and DRG simultaneously, this study will capture the temporal dynamics of immune cell recruitment, keratinocyte differentiation arrest, sensory neuron transcriptional reprogramming, and microbiome succession in a single coordinated framework. Trajectory inference and RNA velocity analyses will define the order in which barrier, immune, neuro-immune, and microbial perturbations emerge, resolving longstanding questions about the primacy of outside-in versus inside-out pathogenesis. Multi-modal factor analysis will integrate scRNA-seq with microbial abundance data to discover microbiome-immune and microbiome-neural gene modules. Top-ranked modules will nominate therapeutic targets that will be validated using pharmacological interventions and genetic tools in the same mouse model, with efficacy measured by itch behavior, skin histology, and single-cell pharmacotranscriptomics.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We will construct a quad-compartment organ-on-a-chip device featuring an intestinal epithelial barrier module connected via a vascular channel to a full-thickness innervated skin equivalent, thereby physically modeling the gut-skin axis in atopic dermatitis. The intestinal compartment will be colonized with AD-associated dysbiotic gut microbiota or healthy control consortia, and microbial metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan catabolites will be transported through the vascular channel to the skin compartment harboring keratinocytes, fibroblasts, iPSC-derived sensory neurons, and immune cells. ScRNA-seq of both skin and gut compartments under dysbiotic versus eubiotic conditions will identify metabolite-responsive transcriptional programs in keratinocytes and immune cells and determine how gut-derived signals modulate neuro-immune crosstalk and barrier gene expression in the skin. This integrated platform will directly test whether specific microbial metabolites are sufficient to drive or ameliorate AD-like phenotypes. Candidate postbiotic or prebiotic interventions will be screened by introducing them into the gut compartment and measuring downstream effects on skin barrier integrity, immune activation, and neuronal sensitization.

label: claude_opus_46
text: Using IL-4/IL-13 transgenic mice that develop spontaneous AD-like dermatitis, we will perform paired scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics on lesional skin to construct a high-resolution cellular and spatial map of neuro-immune niches. Particular focus will be placed on identifying spatially defined microdomains where sensory nerve terminals, mast cells, type 2 innate lymphoid cells, and barrier-disrupted keratinocytes co-localize, hypothesizing that these niches serve as self-amplifying inflammatory units. Ligand-receptor interaction mapping within these niches will delineate signaling circuits involving IL-31, TSLP, substance P, and CGRP that sustain the itch-scratch-inflammation cycle. Concurrent shotgun metagenomics of the skin surface at matched spatial positions will determine whether microbial colonization patterns are structured by these neuro-immune niches. Therapeutic disruption of niche integrity will be attempted using neuropeptide receptor antagonists, anti-IL-31 antibodies, and targeted bacteriotherapy with Roseomonas mucosa, with spatial transcriptomics readouts quantifying niche dissolution and disease resolution at the molecular level.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose generating a humanized skin xenograft mouse model by transplanting full-thickness skin from AD patients and healthy controls onto immunodeficient NSG mice reconstituted with autologous peripheral blood mononuclear cells. This system preserves human-specific barrier architecture, microbiome, immune cell repertoire, and cutaneous innervation patterns that are lost in conventional murine models. Serial scRNA-seq of the xenografted skin at baseline and after challenge with house dust mite allergen will capture patient-specific immune trajectories, barrier protein dynamics, and neuropeptide expression profiles across all four AD pathophysiological domains. Concurrent skin swab metagenomics will track microbiome shifts during flare induction and link specific microbial taxa to transcriptomic changes in keratinocytes and resident immune cells. This personalized disease avatar will be used to test precision therapeutic strategies, including JAK inhibitors, anti-TSLP biologics, and topical microbiome transplants, with treatment response assessed by scRNA-seq-derived pharmacodynamic signatures, thereby enabling mechanism-based treatment selection.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We will develop an AD skin-on-a-chip that incorporates CRISPR-based inducible gene perturbation in keratinocytes, enabling temporally controlled knockdown of key barrier genes (FLG, SPINK5, CDSN) during co-culture with immune cells, sensory neurons, and skin commensals. By sequentially activating barrier defects at defined time points, we can determine the causal ordering of barrier failure relative to immune activation, neurogenic inflammation, and microbial dysbiosis in AD pathogenesis. Each perturbation event will be followed by time-resolved scRNA-seq of all cell types to capture the cascade of transcriptomic changes propagating from barrier-deficient keratinocytes to neighboring immune and neural cells. Microbial community dynamics on the epithelial surface will be monitored by 16S sequencing to establish whether S. aureus expansion is a cause or consequence of barrier-immune disruption. Computational causal inference modeling will integrate these temporal datasets to build a directed acyclic graph of AD pathogenesis, and the most upstream druggable nodes will be targeted with barrier-repair lipid formulations, protease inhibitors, or immunomodulatory agents in the same chip system.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a comparative multi-tissue scRNA-seq study across three complementary transgenic AD mouse models: Flg-knockout, K14-IL-4 transgenic, and K14-TSLP transgenic mice, representing barrier-first, immune-first, and neuro-immune-first disease initiation paradigms respectively. For each model, skin, draining lymph nodes, dorsal root ganglia, and gut-associated lymphoid tissue will be profiled at matched disease severity stages. Cross-model integration using Harmony and LIGER will identify shared and model-specific cell states, gene modules, and cell-cell communication networks, providing a systems-level view of how different initiating mechanisms converge on common AD pathophysiology across all four axes. Concurrent skin and gut microbiome profiling by shotgun metagenomics will determine whether convergent microbial signatures arise regardless of the initiating insult. Shared convergence nodes, particularly those linking barrier failure to neuro-immune amplification loops, will represent robust therapeutic targets. These will be validated by pharmacological intervention across all three models, with treatment efficacy assessed by a unified multimodal disease severity index integrating histopathology, itch behavior, scRNA-seq immune profiling, and microbiome composition.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a multi-target pharmacological strategy combining a dual PYCR1/PYCR2 inhibitor with simultaneous blockade of extracellular proline uptake transporters to overcome all major compensatory resistance axes in proline-dependent cancers. The high active-site conservation (~85% homology) between PYCR1 and PYCR2 enables rational design of a single small-molecule inhibitor using structure-guided optimization of existing fragment hits that occupy both the P5C substrate pocket and the NADH/NADPH cofactor binding site, thereby neutralizing both isoform compensation and cofactor-mediated metabolic rerouting within the mitochondrial matrix. Concurrently, pharmacological inhibition of SLC38A2 (the dominant Na+-dependent proline importer in many tumor types) and SLC6A20 would block compensatory extracellular proline scavenging. This triple-node blockade—dual mitochondrial PYCR and plasma membrane transporter inhibition—would create a synthetic lethal proline deficiency state specifically in cancer cells with high proline demand. The approach is feasible using medicinal chemistry optimization of validated fragment scaffolds for PYCR1/2 combined with emerging SLC transporter inhibitor programs, and can be validated in isogenic PYCR-knockout cell lines supplemented with varying extracellular proline concentrations.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering mitochondria-targeted bifunctional PROTACs that simultaneously degrade both PYCR1 and PYCR2 within the mitochondrial matrix, coupled with genetic or pharmacological blockade of extracellular proline uptake, to achieve irreversible proline biosynthesis ablation. The PROTAC would incorporate a PYCR1/2-binding warhead derived from validated active-site fragments linked to an E3 ligase-recruiting moiety, with a mitochondrial targeting sequence (triphenylphosphonium cation or mitochondrial penetrating peptide) appended to concentrate the degrader at its site of action. Unlike catalytic enzyme inhibitors, degradation removes the protein scaffold entirely, preventing compensatory upregulation of enzymatic activity via increased cofactor availability or allosteric activation. By simultaneously depleting both mitochondrial PYCR isoforms, the approach eliminates the redundant isoform compensation that limits single-isoform targeting. Extracellular proline salvage would be concurrently blocked using SLC38A2-targeting antibodies or small-molecule inhibitors. This strategy is enabled by recent advances in mitochondria-localizing degrader chemistry and can be validated using quantitative mitochondrial proteomics and 13C-glutamine tracing in cancer cell panels.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose that combined inhibition of NADK2 (mitochondrial NAD kinase 2) and extracellular proline transporter blockade constitutes a novel strategy to functionally neutralize PYCR1/2 dependency while simultaneously addressing cofactor compensation and extracellular proline salvage. NADK2 deletion has been shown to render cells proline-auxotrophic by depleting the mitochondrial NADPH pool required by both PYCR1 and PYCR2, effectively disabling both isoforms without requiring direct enzymatic inhibition of either. This upstream targeting of the shared cofactor supply eliminates cofactor-mediated metabolic compensation between NADH- and NADPH-utilizing modes of the PYCR enzymes. To block the extracellular proline uptake that rescues NADK2-deficient cells, we propose co-administration of competitive inhibitors of plasma membrane proline transporters (SLC38A2, SLC6A20, and SLC36A1). The approach leverages the recently solved crystal structure of NADK2 dimers to enable structure-based inhibitor design, and would be validated through isotopologue tracing of proline flux in tumor xenografts. This strategy uniquely exploits the compartmentalized requirement for mitochondrial NADPH in proline biosynthesis as a single pharmacological vulnerability.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a synthetic biology approach using engineered, tumor-targeted lipid nanoparticles delivering multiplexed CRISPR guides against PYCR1, PYCR2, PYCR3, and SLC38A2 simultaneously, thereby eliminating all biosynthetic and uptake routes of proline in cancer cells. While individual knockout of PYCR1 or PYCR2 is compensated by the remaining isoform, and dual mitochondrial PYCR knockout is rescued by cytoplasmic PYCR3 or extracellular proline import, quadruple targeting would create an inescapable proline deficit. The multiplexed guide RNAs would be delivered using ionizable lipid nanoparticles incorporating mitochondrial targeting sequences to ensure efficient disruption of mitochondria-localized PYCR1/2 mRNA as well as nuclear-encoded targets. The NADH/NADPH cofactor compensation is inherently addressed because all three PYCR isoforms—regardless of cofactor preference—are eliminated. Tumor selectivity can be achieved through surface-functionalized nanoparticles bearing tumor-homing peptides or antibody fragments. Feasibility is supported by existing multiplexed CRISPR delivery platforms and can be validated by measuring intracellular proline depletion, redox state perturbation, and tumor growth inhibition in patient-derived xenograft models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the mitochondrial localization of PYCR1/2 by combining a mitochondria-targeted electron transport chain uncoupler with an extracellular proline chelation strategy to simultaneously deplete both the cofactor supply and the proline salvage pathway. Mitochondrial uncouplers such as FCCP derivatives dissipate the proton gradient, collapsing the mitochondrial membrane potential that drives both NADH generation via the TCA cycle and NADPH production via nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT), thereby starving PYCR1 and PYCR2 of both cofactors simultaneously within their mitochondrial compartment. To prevent compensatory extracellular proline uptake, we propose concurrent administration of a prolyl-tRNA synthetase inhibitor analog (halofuginone-related compound) that traps intracellular proline in a non-productive complex, functionally depleting the bioavailable proline pool regardless of source. The dual action of cofactor depletion in the mitochondrial matrix and cytoplasmic proline sequestration addresses isoform compensation, cofactor switching, and salvage pathway resistance in a single regimen. Tumor selectivity is achievable through dose optimization leveraging cancer cells' heightened dependence on mitochondrial proline synthesis under hypoxia and nutrient stress. This can be validated through real-time NAD+/NADH ratio monitoring with genetically encoded biosensors and 13C-proline flux analysis.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing a covalent pan-PYCR inhibitor that exploits a conserved non-catalytic cysteine residue shared between PYCR1 and PYCR2 in the mitochondrial matrix, combined with prolidase (PEPD) inhibition to block collagen-derived proline recycling and extracellular proline scavenging. Covalent targeting would provide irreversible, sub-stoichiometric inhibition of both mitochondrial isoforms simultaneously, overcoming the concentration-limited potency of current competitive inhibitors. The covalent warhead (e.g., acrylamide or chloroacetamide) would be appended to a scaffold occupying both the P5C binding site and the NAD(P)H pocket, addressing cofactor-mediated resistance by physically occluding both substrate and cofactor binding. PEPD inhibition would block the major pathway by which cancer cells recycle proline from collagen degradation products in the tumor microenvironment, preventing compensatory proline scavenging that bypasses biosynthesis blockade. This two-drug combination strategy is feasible because PEPD is a cytoplasmic metalloproteinase amenable to chelation-based inhibitor design. Validation would employ PYCR1/2 target engagement assays using activity-based protein profiling combined with proline isotopologue tracing in 3D tumor spheroid and orthotopic models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a gene therapy approach using adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors encoding a mitochondria-localized dominant-negative PYCR mutant that forms non-functional heteromeric complexes with endogenous PYCR1 and PYCR2, combined with a short hairpin RNA cassette targeting plasma membrane proline transporters. Since PYCR1 and PYCR2 function as homodecamers in the mitochondrial matrix, expression of a catalytically dead mutant retaining the oligomerization interface would poison endogenous enzyme complexes through dominant-negative incorporation, simultaneously neutralizing both isoforms regardless of their cofactor usage. The same AAV construct would encode shRNAs against SLC38A2 and SLC6A20 to block compensatory extracellular proline uptake. Tumor-specific expression would be driven by a hypoxia-response element promoter, leveraging the hypoxic tumor microenvironment where PYCR-dependent NAD+ regeneration is most critical. This single-vector approach addresses isoform compensation through dominant-negative poisoning, cofactor compensation through cofactor-independent enzyme inactivation, and extracellular salvage through transporter knockdown. Feasibility is supported by established AAV manufacturing and the availability of structural data for PYCR oligomeric interfaces, and efficacy would be assessed by measuring tumor proline depletion and growth arrest in immunodeficient mouse models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a metabolic synthetic lethality strategy that pairs PYCR1/2 inhibition with blockade of the mitochondrial glutamate transporter SLC25A22, simultaneously eliminating the mitochondrial substrate supply for proline biosynthesis and disrupting the redox cofactor balance. SLC25A22 imports glutamate into the mitochondrial matrix, where P5CS converts it to P5C—the direct substrate of PYCR1 and PYCR2. Blocking this transporter would starve mitochondrial PYCR enzymes of substrate while also disrupting TCA cycle anaplerosis and the NADH generation that fuels PYCR1-mediated proline synthesis, thus addressing cofactor-mediated compensation at its source. Combined with pharmacological blockade of plasma membrane proline importers to prevent extracellular salvage, this creates a three-pronged metabolic blockade: substrate deprivation, cofactor disruption, and import inhibition. Isoform compensation between PYCR1 and PYCR2 becomes irrelevant because neither enzyme can function without mitochondrial P5C substrate. The strategy can be validated using SLC25A22 knockdown combined with proline transporter inhibition, measuring synthetic lethality through proliferation assays, mitochondrial redox status, and in vivo tumor regression in proline metabolism-dependent cancer models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a strategy that reframes the LSC-versus-HSC selectivity problem as a problem of hematopoietic rescue rather than differential targeting. The approach involves ex vivo harvesting and expansion of patient HSCs prior to or during initial remission, engineering them with lentiviral-delivered drug-resistance cassettes (such as mutant MGMT and cytidine deaminase) using current gene-editing platforms, and then reinfusing these chemoprotected HSCs after administering deliberately myeloablative, non-selective anti-stem-cell therapy. By rendering HSCs resistant to specific cytotoxic agents, the therapeutic index is effectively decoupled from the molecular similarity between LSC and HSC: the therapy can be non-selective and maximally cytotoxic because damage to normal HSCs is preemptively mitigated. Recent advances in ferroptosis-inhibiting ex vivo HSC expansion and base-editing technologies now make high-efficiency, safe gene modification of true long-term repopulating HSCs feasible. The key innovation is combining next-generation HSC expansion protocols with multiplexed chemoprotective gene engineering to enable dose-intensified, non-discriminating stem cell ablation strategies in AML.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the competitive niche-occupancy dynamics between HSC and LSC as a therapeutic lever. Building on evidence that healthy HSPCs can outcompete leukemia-initiating cells for shared bone marrow niches in a dose-dependent manner, we will engineer supraphysiological-fitness HSCs by ex vivo CRISPR-mediated enhancement of niche-adhesion and self-renewal programs—for example, upregulating CXCR4 signaling responsiveness or introducing gain-of-function modifications in c-MPL—then infusing these cells at high dose during chemotherapy-induced remission. The engineered HSCs would preemptively saturate the limited endosteal and vascular niches before residual LSCs can re-engage them, thereby denying LSCs the extrinsic self-renewal signals necessary for disease regeneration. This approach sidesteps the need for LSC-specific molecular targets because it operates through competitive exclusion rather than selective killing. Feasibility is supported by current HSC gene-editing capabilities and validated xenograft models of niche competition. The strategy would be tested in patient-derived xenograft systems and, if successful, translated through existing clinical gene-therapy infrastructure.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose targeting the transient leukemic-regenerating cell (LRC) state rather than therapy-naive LSCs or shared LSC/HSC surface markers. Recent work has demonstrated that chemotherapy effectively depletes LSCs in vivo, but relapse originates from a molecularly distinct, transient LRC population that emerges during the narrow post-chemotherapy window. We will use longitudinal single-cell multi-omics of patient bone marrow collected at precise intervals after induction chemotherapy to define the temporal transcriptomic and epigenomic signature of LRCs across genetically diverse AML subtypes. We will then design combination therapies—timed to the LRC emergence window—using agents that target LRC-specific programs such as inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress response, and de-differentiation pathways, which are not active in quiescent HSCs recovering from chemotherapy. Because LRCs are a therapy-induced, transient state not shared by normal HSCs, this temporal-targeting paradigm circumvents the phenotypic overlap problem entirely. This approach is feasible using existing single-cell platforms and patient-derived xenograft models that faithfully recapitulate remission-relapse kinetics.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose exploiting the differential circadian clock dependency between LSCs and HSCs to create a temporal therapeutic window. Genetic studies have shown that AML LSCs depend on intact circadian clock genes such as CLOCK and BMAL1 for self-renewal and disease propagation, whereas normal HSCs tolerate loss of these same genes. We will systematically map the circadian oscillation profiles of cell-cycle regulators, DNA damage repair enzymes, and apoptotic thresholds in patient-matched LSC and HSC populations using time-resolved single-cell transcriptomics over a full 24-hour cycle. Using these phase maps, we will identify time windows during which LSCs are maximally vulnerable to cytotoxic agents (due to S-phase entry or nadir of DNA repair capacity) while HSCs remain in a protected quiescent or repair-competent state. We will then design a chronotherapeutic regimen that delivers existing chemotherapy at the optimal circadian phase, validated first in AML xenograft models with humanized bone marrow. This strategy requires no new molecular targets—only optimized timing of existing drugs—making it immediately translatable.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a forced-differentiation-plus-immunosurveillance strategy that converts the selectivity problem from a stem-cell-targeting challenge into a differentiation-state-dependent immune recognition problem. Rather than attempting to distinguish LSCs from HSCs by molecular markers, we will use epigenetic differentiation-inducing agents—combinations of LSD1 inhibitors with WNT pathway modulators—to drive LSCs out of the stem cell state into partially differentiated progeny that express lineage-associated antigens and lose immune-evasive properties. Critically, these differentiated leukemic cells acquire neo-antigen presentation and immune-activating ligands that make them susceptible to NK cell and T cell cytotoxicity, while the residual normal HSC pool, which does not bear the oncogenic epigenetic burden, remains in its quiescent niche and is not driven to differentiate by these agents. The innovation lies in coupling differentiation therapy with engineered NK cell infusion timed to the differentiation wave, creating a two-step strategy where neither step alone requires LSC-specific targets. Feasibility is supported by recent preclinical data showing synergy between LSD1 inhibition, WNT perturbation, and immune effector cell-mediated killing in AML models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering synthetic extracellular vesicle decoys that intercept niche-derived self-renewal signals preferentially utilized by LSCs, thereby starving them of microenvironmental support without directly targeting shared surface markers. LSCs hijack the bone marrow vascular and endosteal niche, receiving critical survival cues including miR-126 from endothelial cells, CXCL12 from mesenchymal stromal cells, and Wnt ligands from osteoblasts. We will design biomimetic nanovesicles displaying LSC-relevant receptor ectodomains (CXCR4, Frizzled, c-KIT) that competitively sequester these ligands in the marrow microenvironment. Because LSCs are more dependent on niche-derived signals for maintaining quiescence and self-renewal than normal HSCs—which have more robust cell-autonomous self-renewal programs—this signal interception would disproportionately impair LSC fitness. The decoy vesicles can be engineered using established membrane-protein reconstitution and exosome-mimetic fabrication methods. Efficacy would be evaluated in co-culture systems and patient-derived xenograft models by measuring selective depletion of functional LSCs while preserving HSC repopulating capacity.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a mutation-agnostic synthetic lethality platform that leverages the obligate replicative stress burden of LSCs rather than any specific driver mutation. LSCs, despite their quiescence, carry an elevated burden of replication-associated DNA damage, aberrant R-loop formation, and dysregulated origin firing compared to normal HSCs, reflecting cumulative oncogenic stress from multiple cooperating mutations acquired during leukemogenesis. We will perform genome-wide CRISPR fitness screens comparing the genetic dependencies of primary patient LSC-enriched populations versus matched normal HSCs, focusing specifically on DNA damage tolerance and replication stress response pathways such as ATR-CHK1 signaling, BRCA1-mediated fork protection, and the Fanconi anemia pathway. Hits that are selectively essential in LSCs but dispensable in HSCs will be validated pharmacologically using existing clinical-grade inhibitors of these pathways. This approach does not require identification of new surface markers or individual molecular targets but instead exploits a systemic functional vulnerability emergent from the mutational architecture of LSCs. The platform is feasible with current CRISPR screening technology adapted for primary human hematopoietic cells.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a niche-restorative therapeutic strategy that reverses the leukemia-educated bone marrow microenvironment to one that preferentially supports normal HSC function while becoming inhospitable to LSCs. AML LSCs actively remodel the marrow stroma, vasculature, and extracellular matrix to create a permissive niche, including suppressing osteoblast maturation, increasing vascular permeability, and downregulating chemokines like CXCL14 from mesenchymal stromal cells. We will develop a combination regimen targeting these stromal alterations—using anti-angiogenic agents to normalize leaky vasculature, bone-anabolic agents such as parathyroid hormone analogues to restore osteoblastic niches, and recombinant CXCL14 to re-establish normal stromal signaling—administered concurrently with standard chemotherapy. The rationale is that a restored normal niche will selectively favor HSC engraftment and self-renewal over LSC persistence, effectively turning the microenvironment into a selective filter. Each of these interventions uses clinically available or advanced-stage agents, making rapid translation feasible. Efficacy would be assessed by measuring the LSC-to-HSC ratio in serial bone marrow biopsies and by competitive repopulation assays in xenograft models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a sequential ablate-and-replace strategy using iPSC-derived, leukemia-free HSCs to decouple LSC eradication from HSC preservation entirely. Rather than seeking selectivity between LSC and HSC during therapy, this approach embraces non-selective myeloablation combined with transplantation of patient-derived iPSC-HSCs generated from non-hematopoietic somatic cells such as dermal fibroblasts. Recent advances in iPSC-to-HSC differentiation protocols and clinical-grade iPSC manufacturing now permit generation of engraftable, autologous hematopoietic progenitors free of leukemic mutations. The key innovation is using the patient's own non-leukemic genome as the source of replacement HSCs, avoiding both the graft-versus-host disease of allogeneic transplant and the leukemic contamination risk of autologous marrow harvest. We will optimize directed differentiation protocols to produce iPSC-HSCs with durable multilineage engraftment capacity, validated through serial transplantation in immunodeficient mice. If successful, this strategy would fundamentally bypass the selectivity problem by eliminating the requirement to spare endogenous HSCs during treatment.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering therapeutic stem cells with a bifunctional surface adaptor that reads injury-specific glycocalyx degradation signatures and converts them into homing signals. The adaptor is a recombinant fusion protein comprising a single-chain antibody fragment recognizing the syndecan-1 stub neoepitope (the membrane-proximal core protein domain exposed only after metalloproteinase-mediated ectodomain shedding at injury sites) linked to a high-affinity integrin-binding domain. This construct is displayed on the surface of exogenously administered mesenchymal stem cells via a lipid-anchored protein G intermediary, bypassing genetic modification. Because the syndecan-1 stub is uniquely unmasked in injured endothelium and absent in healthy vasculature bearing intact glycocalyx, the adaptor confers injury-site-selective tethering, firm adhesion, and subsequent transendothelial migration without altering normal glycocalyx barrier function. The design is disease-agnostic, as syndecan-1 shedding is a conserved early response across ischemic, traumatic, and inflammatory injuries. Feasibility is supported by existing antibody-engineering platforms, lipid-anchored cell-surface decoration methods, and demonstrated shedding of syndecan-1 in multiple preclinical and clinical injury models.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a chemokine-gradient amplification strategy at injury sites using injectable, injury-glycocalyx-responsive nanoparticles that locally reconstitute the chemokine-presenting capacity lost through heparan sulfate shedding, thereby creating a selective homing beacon for circulating stem cells. The nanoparticles are functionalized with synthetic heparan sulfate mimetic glycopolymers whose sulfation pattern is tuned to preferentially bind SDF-1/CXCL12 and present it to CXCR4 on stem cells. Crucially, the nanoparticles carry surface-exposed collagen-IV-binding peptides that anchor them exclusively to sub-endothelial matrix exposed by glycocalyx denudation and endothelial retraction at injury sites, preventing off-target deposition on intact endothelium. Once immobilized, the nanoparticles capture circulating or locally released CXCL12 and present it in the haptotactic orientation required to promote stem cell arrest, crawling, and diapedesis. This approach is tissue- and disease-agnostic because collagen-IV exposure and heparan sulfate loss are universal features of vascular injury, and it preserves healthy glycocalyx function elsewhere.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering therapeutic cells with a synthetic glycocalyx coating that enables selective adhesion at injury sites by exploiting the increased exposure of low-molecular-weight hyaluronan fragments generated during glycocalyx degradation. Stem cells are coated ex vivo with cholesterol-anchored glycopolymers presenting multivalent CD44-mimetic peptides that bind low-molecular-weight hyaluronan oligosaccharides with high avidity but show negligible affinity for high-molecular-weight hyaluronan in intact glycocalyx. The resulting cells interact selectively with the hyaluronan fragment-enriched pericellular environment at injured endothelium, promoting initial tethering and activation of integrin-mediated firm adhesion. This approach leverages the well-characterized size-dependent functional switch of hyaluronan, where fragmentation into oligosaccharides of four to twenty-five disaccharides is a conserved damage-associated molecular pattern across ischemia-reperfusion, trauma, and inflammatory injury. The synthetic glycocalyx polymer does not mask endogenous selectin ligands, preserving normal rolling interactions. Feasibility is demonstrated by existing cholesterol-anchored glycopolymer membrane insertion technologies and well-characterized CD44-hyaluronan binding biochemistry.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a bispecific aptamer bridge strategy in which two nucleic acid aptamers are conjugated via a flexible linker: one arm binds the chondroitin sulfate-enriched remnant glycocalyx selectively present at injury sites, and the other binds a surface marker on circulating or infused therapeutic stem cells. Tissue injury characteristically shifts the glycocalyx GAG ratio from heparan sulfate-dominant to chondroitin sulfate-enriched, as heparan sulfate is preferentially shed by heparanase while chondroitin sulfate is relatively preserved. By selecting aptamers through SELEX against chondroitin sulfate-4,6-disulfated motifs that become enriched on injured endothelium, the bridge molecule achieves injury-selective binding without interfering with intact glycocalyx. The stem-cell-facing aptamer recognizes CD90 or CD105 on mesenchymal stem cells, thereby physically tethering them to damaged endothelium. This modular platform is disease-agnostic, as the HS-to-CS compositional shift is a conserved injury signature, and aptamer synthesis is scalable and non-immunogenic, with tunable pharmacokinetics through chemical modifications.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a locally delivered, protease-activated glycocalyx-remodeling enzyme system that selectively enhances stem cell extravasation at injury sites by generating defined neo-GAG structures that promote chemokine presentation and integrin activation. The system consists of recombinant heparanase-III fused to an MMP-2/9-cleavable pro-domain, rendering it enzymatically inactive until it encounters the metalloproteinase-rich microenvironment of the injury site. Upon local activation, the enzyme selectively trims residual heparan sulfate chains to six-to-eight saccharide fragments with specific sulfation motifs known to enhance CXCL12 binding and presentation to CXCR4-positive stem cells, effectively converting the degraded glycocalyx into a chemotactic surface rather than merely a denuded barrier. Because the enzyme is injected systemically in its pro-form and activated only where MMP activity is elevated, it does not alter glycocalyx in healthy vasculature. This strategy is disease-agnostic, since elevated MMP-2/9 activity is a conserved feature of tissue injury, and the resulting enhanced chemokine gradients promote homing of both endogenous progenitors and exogenously administered cells.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles as glycocalyx-targeted homing beacons that precondition injury-site endothelium to recruit subsequently administered therapeutic cells. The vesicles are surface-modified via enzymatic sialylation to display sialyl Lewis X for selectin-mediated rolling, combined with a recombinant heparan sulfate-binding domain that recognizes the truncated, highly sulfated HS stubs retained on injured endothelium after heparanase cleavage. Upon binding at the injury site, the vesicles deliver cargo consisting of SDF-1 mRNA and membrane-anchored VCAM-1, which are transferred to injured endothelial cells, transiently amplifying their capacity to recruit circulating stem cells. This two-stage approach confines the homing signal to sites where glycocalyx degradation has occurred, because the HS-stub-binding domain does not engage intact, full-length HS chains, and the selectin ligands engage only activated endothelium expressing E- and P-selectin. The vesicle-based preconditioning is disease-agnostic and avoids systemic immune activation, and feasibility is supported by established exosome engineering, enzymatic glycan modification, and mRNA cargo-loading techniques.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a glycocalyx-composition-sensing chimeric receptor system for therapeutic cells that triggers integrin activation and transendothelial migration only upon engaging injury-remodeled glycocalyx. The chimeric receptor comprises an extracellular domain with tandem lectin modules: a galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain that binds exposed N-acetyllactosamine on desialylated glycoproteins unmasked by glycocalyx degradation, and a chondroitin sulfate-E binding domain that recognizes oversulfated CS motifs enriched at injury sites. Engagement of both domains simultaneously activates an intracellular ITAM signaling cassette that triggers inside-out activation of beta-1 and beta-2 integrins, converting the cell from a passively circulating state to a firmly adherent one. Because both binding events are required (AND-gate logic), the receptor is not activated by healthy endothelium retaining intact sialylation and HS-dominant glycocalyx. This synthetic receptor can be expressed in mesenchymal stem cells, endothelial progenitor cells, or CAR-like therapeutic cells using standard lentiviral transduction, and the approach is inherently disease-agnostic as both glycocalyx desialylation and CS enrichment are conserved features of vascular injury.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a glycocalyx-mimetic hydrogel depot that is applied at surgical or percutaneous injury access sites and functions as a selective stem cell recruitment patch by presenting injury-mimicking glycan compositions. The hydrogel scaffold consists of a hyaluronan backbone cross-linked with defined low-molecular-weight hyaluronan oligosaccharides and decorated with synthetic heparan sulfate hexasaccharides carrying 2-O and 6-O sulfation patterns optimized for SDF-1 binding and presentation. The depot captures circulating SDF-1 from the injury microenvironment and presents it in an immobilized haptotactic gradient that recruits endogenous CXCR4-positive stem and progenitor cells while simultaneously providing CD44 engagement signals through the hyaluronan fragments to promote arrest and transmigration. The hydrogel is biodegradable over seven to fourteen days, matching the therapeutic window for stem cell homing after injury, and its components are non-immunogenic. This strategy is disease-agnostic and applicable to any accessible injury site, and its feasibility relies on established hyaluronan hydrogel chemistry and commercially available synthetic heparan sulfate oligosaccharides with defined sulfation patterns.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose metabolic glycoengineering of therapeutic stem cells to install azide-tagged unnatural sialic acids into their glycocalyx, followed by click-chemistry conjugation of synthetic glycosaminoglycan-binding peptides that recognize the unique sulfation signatures of injury-remodeled endothelial glycocalyx. Using tetraacetylated N-azidoacetylmannosamine feeding, azide groups are incorporated into stem cell surface sialoglycans without genetic modification. DBCO-functionalized peptides, selected by phage display against heparanase-cleaved, N-sulfated heparan sulfate stubs characteristic of injured endothelium, are then clicked onto the cell surface. These peptides engage the short, highly sulfated HS fragments that remain tethered to syndecan and glypican core proteins at injury sites but are absent from the long, heterogeneously sulfated chains of healthy glycocalyx. The decorated cells exhibit enhanced rolling, arrest, and diapedesis specifically at injured endothelium in flow-chamber assays and in vivo injury models. This approach is disease-agnostic, reversible over the timescale of sialic acid turnover, and fully compatible with current GMP cell manufacturing protocols.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a computational glycomics-guided strategy to identify tissue-injury-specific glycocalyx GAG compositional barcodes and exploit them for precision homing of therapeutic cells via rationally designed lectibodies. First, spatial glycomics using multiplexed GAG disaccharide mass spectrometry and single-cell RNA sequencing of GAG biosynthetic enzymes will be performed across multiple injury models to define conserved injury-associated shifts in HS, CS, and HA chain length, sulfation, and proteoglycan core protein ratios. These data will be used to train machine-learning models that predict injury-discriminating glycan epitopes. Second, lectibodies, engineered antibody-lectin fusion proteins whose carbohydrate recognition domains are computationally designed to bind the predicted injury barcodes with high specificity, will be generated and displayed on stem cell surfaces via sortase-mediated ligation. This two-pronged approach overcomes the limitation of empirical targeting by providing a systematic, data-driven framework for glycocalyx-guided homing that is adaptable across tissues and injury types. Feasibility is enabled by current advances in spatial glycomics, computational protein design, and sortase-mediated cell-surface engineering.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering a nuclear-localized, TRIM21 RING-domain–nanobody fusion (NLS-R-Nb) system that exploits the clustering-dependent activation mechanism of TRIM21 to achieve aggregate-selective degradation within the nucleus. By fusing the RING domain of TRIM21 to a nanobody recognizing an aggregate-specific epitope (e.g., misfolded TDP-43, polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin, or phospho-tau conformers) and appending a strong nuclear localization signal, the construct would be delivered by AAV to neurons. The RING domain activates only upon dense clustering on multimeric substrates, intrinsically sparing monomeric native protein. Once ubiquitinated, aggregates are extracted by the resident nuclear VCP/p97 unfoldase and delivered to nuclear proteasomes for degradation, entirely bypassing macroautophagy. We will validate selectivity via quantitative mass spectrometry of monomer versus aggregate pools, and test efficacy in iPSC-derived neuronal models of TDP-43 proteinopathy and tauopathy. This approach directly addresses the unmet need for aggregate-selective clearance in the autophagy-devoid nuclear compartment.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a pharmacological strategy to enhance the endogenous PML nuclear body–SUMO–RNF4 quality-control axis for clearing nuclear protein aggregates in proteinopathies. PML bodies recruit misfolded nuclear proteins, SUMOylate them via UBC9, and engage the SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 to mark them for VCP/p97-mediated extraction and proteasomal degradation. We will use low-dose arsenic trioxide or interferon-gamma—both clinically available agents that potently induce PML body biogenesis and SUMO conjugation—combined with small-molecule VCP activators to accelerate downstream unfoldase activity. Using CRISPR-engineered iPSC-derived neurons expressing polyQ-expanded ataxin-1, mutant huntingtin, or pathological TDP-43, we will quantify aggregate clearance kinetics and monomer sparing by orthogonal insolubility assays and live-cell imaging. This strategy leverages an evolutionarily conserved nuclear proteostasis hub, requires no genetic cargo delivery, and has a translational advantage through the use of repurposed drugs with established safety profiles.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a two-module genetically encoded system coupling an engineered nuclear disaggregase to a proteasome-targeting degron for the clearance of intranuclear pathological aggregates. The first module is a nuclear-targeted, potentiated variant of the yeast disaggregase Hsp104 (e.g., Hsp104-A503V) that solubilizes amyloid and oligomeric assemblies into proteasome-compatible species. The second module is a co-expressed E3 ubiquitin ligase adapter—a CHIP-NLS fusion—that ubiquitinates freshly solubilized misfolded monomers to direct them to the nuclear proteasome, preventing re-aggregation. Aggregate specificity is inherent: Hsp104 variants preferentially engage non-native, aggregated substrates without affecting natively folded proteins. We will deliver both modules via dual-AAV to cortical and motor neurons in TDP-43 and polyQ disease mouse models, measuring aggregate burden, nuclear proteostasis markers, neuronal survival, and behavioral outcomes. This disaggregation-plus-degradation approach uniquely addresses the nuclear compartment where macroautophagy is absent.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose developing bifunctional chimeric molecules—nuclear SUMOylation-targeting chimeras (NuSTACs)—that redirect pathological nuclear aggregates to the endogenous SUMO-STUbL-proteasome degradation axis. Each NuSTAC would comprise a warhead binding aggregate-specific conformational epitopes (e.g., amyloid dyes or peptide-based aggregate binders) linked to a SUMO-interacting motif (SIM) peptide that recruits UBC9 and SUMO E3 ligases to the aggregate surface. Induced polySUMOylation of the aggregate would then engage STUbLs such as RNF4 and TOPORS, which ubiquitinate the substrate and recruit VCP/p97 for unfoldase-assisted proteasomal degradation. Because this pathway operates endogenously in the nucleus and is naturally aggregate-responsive, NuSTACs would exploit the physiological quality-control network without requiring autophagy. We will use structure-activity relationship studies guided by computational docking to optimize aggregate selectivity and nuclear permeability, and validate the platform in iPSC-derived neuronal models of Huntington disease and spinocerebellar ataxia.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose engineering a nuclear-targeted, J-domain protein (JDP) fusion construct inspired by the yeast nuclear disaggregase Apj1, which cooperates with HSP70 to solubilize intranuclear aggregates for proteasomal turnover. By designing a chimeric human JDP bearing a nuclear localization signal and fused to a conformation-selective nanobody that recognizes misfolded aggregated species, we would create a biased disaggregase–ubiquitin–proteasome coupling system. The nanobody would recruit the JDP-HSP70-HSP110 disaggregase machinery specifically to pathological aggregates in the nucleus while ignoring natively folded monomers. HSP70-dependent unfolding would then feed disaggregated polypeptides to the nuclear 26S proteasome. We will express the construct via neuron-tropic AAV in transgenic mouse models of nuclear polyglutamine diseases and TDP-43 proteinopathy, quantifying aggregate clearance, monomer preservation, transcriptional rescue, and neuronal viability. This approach uniquely reconstitutes a metazoan-compatible nuclear disaggregase-to-proteasome pipeline for aggregate-selective clearance.

label: claude_opus_46
text: We propose a strategy exploiting engineered nuclear condensate bodies as aggregate-processing centers that concentrate disaggregation and degradation machinery around pathological nuclear inclusions. We will create an optogenetically controlled, phase-separating scaffold bearing a SUMO2-interaction module and an HSP70-binding domain, tagged with a nuclear localization signal. Upon light activation, the scaffold nucleates transient condensates that co-recruit misfolded aggregate-prone proteins (via SUMO2-SIM interactions with SUMOylated aggregates), the HSP70-HSP110-DNAJB1 disaggregase triad, and proteasome complexes. After disaggregation and proteasomal degradation within these synthetic condensates, the scaffold dissolves upon light withdrawal, restoring normal nuclear architecture. We will test this system in HEK293 and iPSC-derived cortical neuron models expressing polyQ-huntingtin or mutant TDP-43, measuring aggregate clearance kinetics by live imaging and solubility assays. This approach creates a programmable, reversible intranuclear proteostasis hub that bypasses autophagy entirely.

label: claude_opus_46
